This Company was formed on the sth March, 1892, for the purpose of acquiring and working the business then carried on in Warrington and elsewhere by the well-known firm of Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton, as General Ironmongers and Wholesale Merchants, and it was then considered that the shares should be limited only to the members of the firm and some of their employas. but inasmuch as Mr. W. Skelton is in failing health (which compels him to retire from all busi- ness and leave the district), they have determined to Issue shares to their customers and the public.

On the amid Mr. W. Skelton's retirement three other directors will be appointed, which will make the number of directors foar. Mr. William Fairhurst, of Latchford, Mr. Henry Roberts. of Warrington, and Mr. W J. Foreshow have been nominated, and have agreed to accept the nomination. The business comprises dealing in Ironmongery. Hard- ware, Cycles, Smailwares, Toys, Brushes, Fancy Goods. foreign importing and exporting of general goods. Together with the business the Company will acquire: All the freehold land and building known as Jubilee Buildings, Horsemarket-et., Warrington aforesaid, which is subject to an annual chief rent of £75, and valued by Mr. John E. Wright. of Warrington, at £5,100; also the Stock-in-trade, Machinery, Work Tools, Fixtures, and Effects now used or employed in connection with the Bald business, and valued by Mr. Thomas Sutton, of Warrington, as at the let of Janu- ary, 1892; at £10,415 Ss.. and the book and other debts amounting to £5,600, and the benefits of all contracts and engagements subsisting in the said business on July let, 1892. Copies of these valuations appear below. The Company will also take over as and from the Ist day of July, 1892, the tenancy of the warehouse, tenement, building, and premises now ocsupied by Messrs. W. r. and W. Skel- ton, Limited, at Whitechapel, Liverpool, at the rent of £7O per annum. The Company will also acquire the good-will trade-marks, and the vendors' interest in all patents used in the said business. . . . . . _ _

The capital necessary for the acquisition and working of the business and for the freehold land, shop, good-will, naaehinery, stock, book debts. Ac., is estimated to be E 25.000. The books of the concern have been examined by Mr. Arthur Bennett, chartei eat accountant. Warrington, for the last four-raid-a-half years, His certificate shows that the average aggregate net profits, after making due allowance for depreciation, amounted to £3,127 us. Mr. W. P. Skelton, under whose management the business has so prospered, and who is retaining the whole of his interest in the business in ordinary shares, has agreed to act as managing director for a period of ten years, and Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton have entered into an agreement with the company not to carry on or be interested in any compet- ing business in Warrington, or within a distance ot 60 miles thereof. The progress of the business has been uninterrupted for many years, and there is not any reason why it should not continue to increase with the growth of the locality having more than trebled during the past six years. The Warrington premises are in the best position in the town, daily increasing in value, and the Liverpool Branch especially is capable of much development, and suitable 'premises have been secured at a low rent in a first-rate busi- ness locality. (b) An Agreement dated the 4th day of April. 1892. and made between the said W. P. Skelton and Wilfred Skelton of the Ist part, the said Charles Humphreys of the 2nd part, and the Company of the 3rd part, • adopting the last-mentioned Agreement on the part of the Company. (r) An Agreement dated the Tenth slay of September, 1892, and made between the said W. P. Skelton and W. . . _

In addition to the above-named Agreement there are vari- ous trade contracts, and all applicants for shares shall be deemed to have bad notice of these contracts or engagements, and to have waived all right to any particulars thereof, whether under section 38 of the Companies Act, 1867, or otherwise. Copies of the Memorandum and Articles of Association and of the above-mentioned Agreements, Valuations, and Certi- ficate of accountant may be Inspected at the offices of the Solicitors of the Company.

COPIES OF THE VALUATIONS REFERRED TO. Warrington. May 10th, 1892. VALUATION OF SHOP AND WAREHOUSE, /sc., situate in Horsemarket-street, belonging to Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton. Limited. Having inspected this property. I beg to report as follows, viz.:—

• The whole of the premises cover an area of 493 square yards, or thereabout, and is freehold subject to an annual rental of £75, payable t,o Lord Winmarleigh. The main building covers an area of about 262 square yards. It is three storeys high, with good basement under the whole area, and attic formed in roof. The shop has a frontage to Horsemarket-street of 56 feet. and a clear depth back of over 42 feet ; the two show rooms above are the same size. The property is well and substantially built, and is com- paratively new, having been erected only five years. In addition there is a good yard, about two-thirds of which is covered with glass, also a two sWrey warehouse adjoining same. I estimate the value of the whole property to be five thousand and one hundred pounds.

Yours truly, JOHN EDWARD WRIGHT. Surveyor and Valuer. Warrington. June 16th, 1892. Having gone over the Stock-in-tr Ade, as it now stands, of Messrs. W. AND CHLORIDE OF LIME. May I suggest, in face of the Smallpox in Warrington and Manchester, that all house- holders flush their gullies with a dolly-tubful of water twice a week, and after doing so, put a table-spoonful of Chloride of Lime in the gully, and one in the closet.
I have added Chloride of Lime to stock, and to enable it to be used freely, will supply it at 20. per lb., or tbs. for qd.
Attention to this will at least keep clean and sweet these sources of bad smells.
Yours respectfully,

DOMESTIC Femerrv.—A well-known authoress gives it as an item of domestic, felicity that the man of the family should be absent at least six hours a day. "I HAVE learned the profound truth," says Alderman Johnson, "from eating turtle, that it shows a most depraved taste to mock anything for its greenness." An analysing dame reporte that "she had heard of but one old woman who kissed her cow; but , she knows of many thousands of young ones who I have kissed very great calves." PERSEVERANCE.—" Your son, madam, persists in doing nothing," says the director. "Then," replies the woman, by no means disconcerted, you should give him the prize for perseverance." YoUNG WIPE--" Why, John, take care; don't hold the baby that way. You men are no earthly good at tending children." Young husband— , " Julianinski, I believe that baby would cry if F stood it on its head in the corner I It's incorri- gible." AN English admiral being about to engage a Spanish vessel, thus addressed his men My: good fellows, never let it be said that we, who• live on prime beef and mutton, were beaten by; those who have nothing to eat but oranges and; lemons." A DEVOTEE of Bacchus thus addressed his hat, which had fallen from his head: "If I pick you up, I fall; if I fall you-Will not pick me up—then I leave yon," and he staggered proudly away. People kept away until it was found that the next-door neighbour knocked the ashes out of hie pipe at that time. "That's no excuse," replied the judge. "You are not likely to hear good English at the bar." A LADY had in her employ an excellent girl who had one fault—her face was always grimy. Mrs. X., wishing to tell her to wash her face without offending her, at last resorted to strategy. "1)o you know, Bridget," she remarked in a confidential manner, "that if you wash your face every day in, hot soap and water it will make you beautiful." " Will it ? " answered the wily Bridget. "Sure, it a wonder ye never tried it, me.'arn I" 7 Two men were out shooting the other day; one had a license—the other hadn't. A keeper approached, and the one that hid a license ran away. The keeper was a good runner, and an exciting chase ensued over a sidle and a half of nice ploughed fields. , At last the keeper got up to the runaway. "Now, sir, where's your license ?" It was produced. " Then why did you run away ? " " Oh, I'm "fond of exercise," answered the mm; "but don't you think you'd better ask my friend if he has one!" A WELL-TO-DO MAN was Dr. Osgood, parson of 'the First Church. In his time Springfield was a mere village and Indian Orchard a sheep pasture. :The parson owned the main portion of that ward, • conducted it us a farm and sheep ranch, and • employed John Corey and his wife to run it. The parson drove out to view his possessions one day, ...sand found old Corey drunk, beating his wife. 76 Well, well, Mr. Corey," said the parson, "a man -whipping his wife !" Yes. "Mr. Corey, recollect Y.r-"thal woman is the weaker vessel." Well, let her carry less sail, then."—The Argonaut. The "Daily Chronicle" says :—What 2, hullabaloo there would he among the " classes " were the Government to decide to send 2,000 workingmen to the World's Fair, and thence for a tour of tn e prin- cipal cities of Lho United States. Yet this is the latest feat in civilisation of little Japan, which certainly has nothing to boast of in the way of surplus cash, while Tokio is much further from Chicago. than is Loudon. As Mr. Kipling sinus, " 011-east is east, and west is west, and never the twain shall meet," but the west might do worse sometimes than take a leaf out the book of the progressive east. ..._

Mr. W. G. Thorpe has some stories of clerical life in his volume just published "The Still Life .of the Middle Temple " (H. Bentley and Son). One is of a simple country clergyman who was recently marry- ing a couple, or rather preparing to do so, a pleasant faced neatly-dressed damsel being present as the most prominent figure. The Rector could net make I;er out, and asked the bridegroom, "Is that the bride ?" " Non zur, she bain't ; I wish she wor." Little contretemps often occur, says M. NEW IOO.K, &c. " Memoirs of a mother-in-law" is the title of a. new novel by that versatile author, Mr. George R. Sims. It is brilliantly. written, and details life as siton from the mother-in-law's point of view. The 'Articular mother-in-law is so admirably defined as to soon become in the reader's mind a livingyeality, andihe'account of her sayings and doings grows more and more interesting. Ererychapter has its tale to tell of her multiform experiences with her children, and their better, or, as the case may be, orser halves. Mr. Sims muet -be complimented upon his close observation, and fertility of resotiree. The memoirs are published by George Newnes, Limited, the paper and printing being excellent and the binding bright and handsome. In the" Golden Treasury series," published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., price 2s. ed., we have to hand Sir Thomas Browne's "Religlo Medici,"' ••• Letters to a friend," and " Christian moralist." This admirable edition of what may be regarded as an English classic is edified by W. A. Greenhill, M.D., whose preface shows that he has devoted a no small amount of care and time to making himself familiar with all that was to be known about the origin of this eetraordinary werk. The fact that the" Reggio' Medici," was written not with the intention ot publication, ;but for private, interest and benefit,expleins the thoroughness and earnestness which mark every page of the work. Mr. Greenhill gives an account of the various additions and emendations which the book has undergone by various editore,, and furnishes a chronological table of dates connected with Sir Thomas Browne. There are copious notes, critical and explana- tory, besides a full index so that the reader uts full value for lits 'Money. He :will not fail •to to struck throughout as much with the good sense as with the quaintness of style. Here is a sentence, for instance, which might at times be remembered with advantage: —" A man may be in as just possession of truth as of a city, and yet be forced to surrender. "I was coming up the road when I was taken sud- denly ill," says a man, describing a memorable expe- rience, and— '

But it will be better to let him give the whole story, which he has done in the form ',of a condensed state- ment, as follows [Co.) I, Joseph T athani, of Folley House, Darley, near Derby, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows : " Up to July, 1881, I Was a strong healthy man, and r never had a day's illness. One night In July (ten years ago) Iwas coming up the road wheal was taken :ad !oily ill. Pains took me aaat entre in the stomach and back. I was barely half a mile from home, but had great diffi- culty and pain in reaching my house, and I never got:oLt again for sixteen weeks. For some time before my seizure I was tired, languid, and out of sorts. I had a bad taste in the mouth, a poor appetite, and Pain after eating. My mouth filled with slimy phlegm which Covered my teeth and mouth, and a dull sinking feeling , came over me. After my sudden seizure I had dread- ful pains in my right side which affected my hip and 'down the leg. The pain was so bad that I could not stand or put my feat to the ground, otherwise I should have fallen. Added to this the pain in' my sides and back was something cruel, for I could not rest either in or out of bed. For weeks I never slept (only dozed now and then), and whatever Was done gave me no relief. I took nitre, turpentine, and all kinds of medicine that I heard tell of, I was also rubbed with embrocations, some of which cost two shillings a bottle. I' saw a doctor , and toOk his medicine, but nothing did me any good: Al! the things I took never seemed to reach the complaint. I got a recommendatiom +and Went as indoor patient At the Derby Infirmary W era l'. was, seeaby &Waal doctor ar.d received great kindness and attention: After being under treatment six weeks I name out as bad as ever. I , next werti to the Buxton Convalescent Hospital and was - theil,undcr, the dostoce and taking the waters for ,three weeks." When I returned fwas a little better, but after a few weeks at 'mine was as bad as ever, and again I went' ta'the'Buxton hospitai, where I was under treat- ment for three weeks. After my return I soon lased into my old state, and I got weaker and weaker. In this state I continued for fourteen months, dung which time In°4wOrlinean-hlair. I was at titb in such agony that for weeks. and weeks I never werit.:S.° bed, for I found no rest there, and I laid down on the sofa in the sitting-room. After suffering ;,,in this way for fourteen months I began to despair of ever getting strong again, when hi' dePteniber, 1882j1 met with a lady, friend who asked::ste 11f I had tried a medicine called Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup. She told nas of rthe benefit she had derived from this medicine, and strangly urged me to give it a trial. I procured a bottle from Mr. Hardhill's, Chemist, Peter Street,.Derby, and commenced taking it. After taking the Syrup for three weeks I felt free from pain, my appetite returned and my food agreed with nie, and I gained strength every day. I was so dreadfully weak that it took a long time before I got up my strength, but I was soon back at my work, and although it is nine years since, have never ailed since from my old complaints. I keep the Syrup in the house, and if ever I feel that I require a dose of medicine I take it,and it always seta -md..right. Mr. Tatham is a man of sterling worth and has worked at the Evans Paper Mills, Derby, for over ten years. Now. let us understand why he was taken ill suddenly. Nature never does anything without a sufficient reason. and althoues Mr. Tatham dcee pot give the details of his previous life we know that in some way—innocently and insensibly no doubt—he brought his system into a condition to in- duce a sharp attack of indigestion, and dyspepsia, which then threw. his nerves into wild disorder, filled his blood with poison, and undermined his manly vigour. Thou- sands are doing thiu without taking notice of the early symptoms of this prevalent and dange.rous malady— viz., bad breath, foul taste in the.raciuth, headache, loss. of appetite, coated tongue, yellow skin, depression of Spirits, flashes of heat and cold, pains in the chest,sides, and back, &c. Forewarned is forearmed. "HIS -NAME IS-JOHN."

That name has been pronounced over more: in- fants, probably, in the nations whtch have a history, than any other on.g.• Its simple and compounded forms are met with in many lang.unges and through. all centuries. The Welcome the name has found among all peoples is.a marveli Who can tell the reason for it ? In the early Hebrew. two words meaning" one whom Jehovah Johanan or johohannii; then John or Jonathan, kindred alike in form and meaningi introduce the name. Twenty- nine persons by Old Testament records bore this name, and seven in the New Testament. The Semi- tic root hem nithiCh • Jobm tame yielded similar names, as Hanna and Ilnnnial, in Phcenician. "It appears also," iltys a modern' scholar, "in Japanese, Arabic, Sanscrit,.and in a wide range of African languages." The pleasing significance of the name appears also in the Greek, in the name Theodore; in 'Latin, Deodatus. The heathen theosophy pre, , fixed the name of the deity who made the gift, as Apolloclorus. Diralcrus, Helioclorus, Hermo-• (torus, Pythodorns, and seores of others. John the Baptiser,. so named •by the angel, was hence. I specially, attractive to Jewish motherhood. So I many were called John that appellatives were needed to know one fromanother. Hence John the Baptisi, John the Evangelist, John the Eeveiator; • &c. Later special gifts and offices made the dis- tinctions, as John Chrysostona. (golden month), John Chrysolorous (gold swan); John Phihmouns (labour-loving), and many others. The Greeks wrote it ionanes, the :Romans, Johannes. The Italian spelling is Giovanni ; the French, Jean (Zhan> ;- the Spanish, Joan ; the Portuguese. Joao. Jehan is the Belgian form; Johan the Swiss, Jan the Welsh ; Ivan the Russian, (seven mars having borne it) ' Joyan the Sclavonic Shawm. Irish ; lan, Gallic. A. ramble- in the Sandwich /lands read Kegni on the gunlock of a lianaka, and learned that was hia word for John. The German and Dane write it Hans.

THRILLING LOVE STORY: By LAtrni JEAN LIED=

[T. order that new readers may begin with the foilowieg instalment of this story, and understand it justthe same as though they had read it all from the beginning, we-here give a synopsis of that por- tion of it which has already been published: lonie Lawrence, a poor but beautiful girl, who worked in a large establishment in Now 'fork, won the love (without knowing it) of Aithur Rochester, her em- ployer's only son, who had saved her life at the risk of his own: and because Arthur would not promise to give lonie up, his father disinherited him, and drove him from his home. He went at once to Rini% deelared his love, and asked her to be his wife. But lonie refused him, because she loved Frank Lyons, a worthless adventurer. Fortunately she discovered the true character of Lyons in time to escape marriage with him. She also discovered that she was the niece of Col. Whitney, of Pitts- burgh, who took her home and declared that she should be his heiress, he having no children of his own. His mansion—Beechvale—was presided over by Miss Carriscourt, an accomplished lady, under whose care he placed his new-found niece. Frank Lyons followed lonie to Pittsburgh, and determined to win her for his wife—by foul means, if not by fair. But Arthur Rochester was in the employ of Col. Whitney, and lonia learning to love him dearly, they were betrothed. The events which followed are detailed in the following chapters.

"IT IS Iqo HORRIBLE DREAM," SUE MOANED. "I HAVE PROMISED TO GIVE UP MY LOVER AND WED ANOTHER." A sharp convulsive shudder passed over Co!onel Whitney's strong, stalwart frame. "A week ago, to-day, lonie," he repeated, faintly. "I was a different man; life seemed worth the living, and now it is a torture to me to see the light of each coming day. "Bat to break into the subject while I have the courage," he cried, desperately., "As you recollect, I stayed all day, and all the evening, too, in town. I. met a party of friends when I dropped into a Cafe to dine, and upon their urgent request, joised them. The hours flew by, as bonrs of social plea- sure will, and on leaving the cafe, I can never tell how it happened, I fell into a spirited dispute with one of the gentlemen; bitter words followed. "I had not traversed half the distance, when, directly across my path, I stumbled upon the form of a man, almost buried in the deep drifts. "As it was a bitterly cold night, my first Impression was that the man had lost his way, sunk exhausted by the road side, and had frozen to death.

"In an Instant I was kneeling beside bin), Intent upon rendering him every a.ssistance In my. power. " With a horrible cry, I drew ,it forth, the warm life-blood spurting up in my face as ' I , did so; and as I held it in my hand in that awful moment I heard hurried steps approach—some one stopped short in the path. There was an exclamation of horror, a heavy hand fell on my shoulder, and a voice cried hoarsely in my ear: 'For Heaven's sake, Colonel Whitney, what is thik that you have done 7" I raised my eyes, and saw Mr. Frank Lyons. "In a few breathless words I explained the situa- tion. He shook his head.
"'I was on the steps of the caf6, as were many others, when you two gantlemen parted company,' he said. 'We all heard that bitter quarrel, and now I have witnessed the result of it.'

"I sprang to my feet, white as death. 'ln Heaven's name, you do not mean to insinuate that I—that I—' I could not utter the words for very horror. "'This is your work, he Said, coolly. 'What my eyet3 beheld as I came suddenly upon you, my heart must believe. No denial can avail you. Any law in the land will pronounce you guilty; and jou can yealise for yourself the end.' "In vain I expostulated, vowing nay innocence; yet, as in a glass darkly, I saw for myself just how matters stood.

"• I would be your friend if could,' he -went on. 'I am sorry for you. Flight is your only hope. Go to your home now. To-morrow I will call upon you, and we will advise together. No one knows—no one save myself could condemn you. :You are safe if my lips are closed.' " Protesting my innocence vehemently, I turned away. For long hours after I reached home, I paced the 2oor like a man driven mad. I could see my- self arraigned—the trial on circumstantial evidence, and what the verdict must be. i was a proud man, lonic.. • Some questionthen arose as to the licenses to be given up if the new licenses were granted, and eventually Mr. Davies said., "Ater, consulting 'Mr. Down, that. for the new license in Battersby-lane, they would give up the Fox, the White Bear, and the Currier? Mr. P.. Davies object,ed to this license. ^He contended that if a full license weregranted. to any'house in that neighbourhood it should be<granted to the-Grove, which was a very suitable house, and had a bostling green at- tached to it. An application for one ,for the Grove had been made for 16 or 1.,.7 years. In 1.888 a full license to the• Grove was granted, but it was not con- firmed at the adjeurned licensing sessions. If Mr. Robert Davies's application were granted,Mrs.Beard, the tenant of the Grove, would 'be robbed of her living, because the proposed house would be almost immedi- ately opposite the Grove. 'He +knew why -the license granted in 1288 tothe Grove was not confirmed, but he would not give the reason. r 11.,: Messrs. Greenall and Company would put Mrs. Beard in the house they pro- posed to build they would act in a handsome manner; it would be a quid profuo. Everything would be taken from Mrs. Beard if the present application were granted. Alderman Ohandiey remarked treat the giving up of other licenses was a great object with the beneinand had influenced their conduct throughout. ' Mr. P. Davies added that the working-men of the locality were in favour of Mrs. Beard having the license. Ile thought it would be .unlair to hike it from 41or and give it to Messrs. Greenati. Alderman Holmes objected to the use of the word unfair," and Mr. Davies said he would withdraw it if they could supply him with a better one to express his meaning. (Laughter.) Mr. Chorlton thew ook objection to the granting of both licenses. He said that a personal inquiry had 'been made at the Barracks as to the opinion of the officers on the question. Twenty-four of them had expressed an adverse opinion to the granting of the license, and they comprised the commanding °racer and several captains, as well as a large number of non-commissioned offieert. Eleven property owners in Battersby-lane and the ad- joining streets disapproved of the granting of the license, as well as 209 householders who had appended i their signatures to a memorial against the granting of the license. John Senior said he lived in Scott-st., and was a blacksmith. He had talked with the men employed at , the Waggon Works, and their opinion was that a license 1 •ought not to be granted, as there was no necessity for an hotel. Adam Horrocks, 25, Irlam.st., said he had property in Birchall-st., and he contended that there was no need to erect .an hotel. If people wanted beer it was to be had in the neighbourhood, and if they wanted spitits they would not have far to go. In answer to Mr. Davies, witness said that if a person bad to walk from Sankey Bridges to Padgate for a drink, it would not be a great way. (Laughter.) Riohard Storey said that during the last two or three weeks he had made special visits to the neighbourhood. He had called upon 150 people and ascertained their feelings with regard to the proposed new house, and the greater number of them declared that they did not want one. Joseph Wibberley said he called at 200 houses and got 80 signatures against the new house.—ln answer to Mr. Platt, the witness said the general opinion of those who did not sign was that if they were to have a house at all it should be supplied by Mr. Bolton,who,they contended, ought to have the first chance. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) ' With regard to the proposed new house in Catherine- st., John Fieldhouse said he had visited from 150 to 180 persons and ascertained whether the people approved of a public-house being erected. He got expressions of opinion against the proposed public-house from 100 people who gave him their signatures. He got expres- sions of opinion against it from those who would not append their signatures to a memorial. The opinion of the wives of the workingmen was divided on the ques- tion. Some women were in favour of a public-house, but a large number were against it.—By Mr. Percy Davies : It was the general opinion that if the license were granted at all it should be given to Mrs. Beard, of the Grove. Mr. Edwin Wright, said that he had inquired of 100 persons and the prevailing opinion was against Messrs. Greenail putting up a new house. In answer to Mr. P. Davies, he said the feeling was that if there was to be a license Mrs. Beard should have it.
MR. CHORLTON'S ADDRESS. Mr. Chorlton then addressed the Bench in opposition to the granting of the licenses. He said that since the last meeting of the Bench extraordinary exertions had

1 been m le by Mr. Davies in getting up evidence which he diil not think it necessary to bring on the previous onieision. On the last occasion \fir. Davies relied on the evidence of the genzleinen who prepared the plans, and stated that there was a large ainottut of property in the intmediane vicinity, and that a fully licensed house ought lobe provided in each place. It was 'clear that the Beech did not decicie on the evidence unless they knew wints which Mr. Davies Failed to prove. He was obliged to believe that the offer welch had been made by Messrs. Greenall had had some efteCt, -probably the effect of searing for them the granting of the two licenses they &eked for. But the wantsof the neighbourhood must be coneidered as well as the character of the, applicants. Ar. Davies had brought evidence front die Waggoa Works, but front nowhere else ; not a single witness from the barracks had been called. That was not the' wity to show the wants of the neighbourhood. Sir Gil- bert Greenall was a iarge shareholder in the Wae,goni Works. No doubt The inert from the Waggon Works' who had been called spoke the truth as far as they were concerned, butthey presented a small proportion of the people living in the district. At the barracks they lied a numb& of item free from the sanctities of home life, and the protection which home life afforied. They came oat full of animal life, and what they cenald nde get to drink in the canteen they got eutiitle, and then went back 'to punishment. Lie asked on ilsehalf of the soldiers that the reasonable provision which was made at the Barracks sheuld be sufficient. But he went on wider grounds. Fie appealed to the Bench on behalf of the men and women who worked heed and made long tilers, with great difficulty many times supporting bare lite, he asked that their, cirournetances should be considered. Would the youths. of the neighbourhood be anybetter if public-houses were put eipqn the district? The case of the Bewsey-road license rested on the same footing, and no necessity had been shown for the erection of a public-house there. How did ell this come about? He would not call it a bribe, , belt vex offer made under suspicious circumstances. What were those circumstances? One would think bis friend was under the impression that there was no common sense on the Bench when he referred to the. *houses it was proposed to give up. There were three 'houses together,and did anyone mean to say that taking Vivo down and enlarging the third would depreciate the 'Custom? It was only a giving up on paper. The houses -were not paying, could not Tay, three together, unless the town was besotted with drink. There was bargain- inn there if they liked. The profit would be with Messrs. Greenall. Was the monopdly at present existing onthe part of Messrs. Greenall to be encouraged? He had never, heard of such an offer as that which had been made by the firm, and he asked the Bench to rise to the responsibilities of that day when they were told by this huge monopoly that there were houses which they did not want to keep. The tendh-sheald surely say "We will remember that. As to the new houses, they had not been assured that there was a want for them. He asked the Bench, in conclusion, to protect theims, band and wife and the 'children, and to see that they were brought up in the way they should go, so that there would bane cauee /for blame in the years to come. In conclusion, he asked them to show to the world that the Bench of Warrington wns not to be affected by the offer of a bribe, or whatseemed a bribe, but that they would judge each case according to its merits, and ac- cording to strict justice. ,Mr. P. Davies also reatie e brief address against the which was again supported by Mr. R. I Davies.

George Barker James Cooper., who stands committed for the wilful murder of his wife, seems toqse living in a most luxuriant manner, whicheof course,,is permissible so long as his friends pay for bis food. %Hs meals are applied from Falcon Cliff Hotel, and Cooper, who has tlaee meals a day, has a keen appetite. and is very fastid:ous. He does not read much, but spoxds the greater part of the day in smoking and exercise. The trial of Cooper before a deemster and special jury will take place on Tuesday, the 27th :,lest.. the Attorney- General (Sir James Gall) prosecuting on behalf of the Crown. Mr.. G. A. Ek3g,,, who, along 'with Mr. Thomas Kneen, will defend, hat returned to the island, and has consulted with Mr. Kneen as to the defence. IAT.ILITIES ON TEIE WORKS.
INQUESTS AT LATCHFORD.

•An inquest was held on Saturday at the Ship Canal Hospital, L9.tchfor4.l, on the body of William Taylor, foreman labourer, who mot his death through injuries received whilst at work at Acton Grange, on the 12th of September. The coroner Was Mr. H. C. Yates.—Rebecca Caviar, Wilderspml-roid, wife of the deceased, stated that her husband was 64 years of age. On the 12th of the 'present month he left home early in the morning to go to work. She heard of his being injured about nine o'clock the same morning. She caine to the hospital, tad remained with her husband until his death, which took place on the 15th. The deceased made the follow- ing statement to her :—" There were three men away from work on the morning of the 12th, and I went to bring some waggons down the incline. There were four waggons at the top of the incline. I uncoupled two of them, expecting that the other two were spragged. The two first waggons were set in motion, but the two other waggons also came running down the incline, with the result that I lost control of the brake, and was jambed between the stage and the waggons." The deceased was conscious to the last. He had been accustomed to the work all his life. Other witnesses gave evidence, after which a verdict of" Accidental death " was returned. Mr. Yates then held an inquiry touching the death of a Mitt unknown who was killed at Runcorn on Friday. William Smith, engine driver, stated that he was running his engine at about four miles an hour. when the de- ceased stepped out on to the line and was run over by a ; waggon attached to the front of the engine.—William, Hulse stated that the engine driver whistled twice be- fore the man went en the line. The engine was stopped before it could pass over the man's body.—Henry Riciterhan said that he knew the deceased by the name , of "Richard the Bevil." Be was a tramp, and worked now and then en the canal works.—The Coroner com- plimented the driver on his carefulness, and the jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."

div.head: COMPANY AND ITS RATES.
div.p: THE COMPANY AND ITS RATES.

The following appears in the "Pall Mall Gazette": The railway companies have all been dealt with under the Railway and Canal Traffic Act of 1888;and untrss further extension of time be required—and we think it will not—the new powers will come into operation with the new year. The canal companies also have, with one exception, deposited schedules, and will be dealt with similarly by the Board of Trade and by Parliament. The exception is that of the Manchester Ship Canal, and con- sidering the part its promoters have assumed as pioneers and champions of cheap traffic it may be thought rather surprising that they should now defy the provisions of a law which they took so much tmble and spent so munh money to helpto get, and especially to apply with the utmost rigour to the railway companies."

div.head: PROGRESS OF THE WORK.
div.p: PROGRESS OF THE WORK.

Considerable progress with the Ship Canal is now be- ing made at the Manchester end, and thence on to the , Warrington neighbourhood, where the work, practically speaking, is all but finished, The result is that the number of navvies and others formerly engaged about here has been greatly reduced. A proportion of them have gone toChesterfield to try and obtain employment in connection with the making of the new cross-country railway, andthere are some houses empty in Latchford —formerly so crowded with navvies. Railway deviations and swing bridges are also in an advanced state. AN ADVENTURE ON THE CAN. A party of axeursionists from Liverpool and Manches- ter who ieftthe Liverpool landing stage on Friday after- noon had rather an unpleasant adventure on the Ship Canal. Everything went well on the Manx Fairy until the locks were entered at Saltport, but when the little steamer was about to turn round with the view of mak- ing for the Mersey, a chain which had beendeft loose by a dredger got entangled in the Manx Fairy's propeller. All efierts to clear the screw proved futile. In fact, the steamer could not be moved one way or the other, owing to the obstructiOn. Two-thirds of the passengers were put ashore in boats. and they made the best of their way to Rancorn, to return by train. The rest of the party hailed a steam flat named the Thomas, and they were by means of this taken to Eastham locks. Here the flat was taken in tow by one of the Shropshirellnion tugs, which conveyed the lumbering craft to the Liverpool landing-stage, where the excursionists lacded shortly before eleven o'clock the same night.

div.head: RIXTON BRIDGE.
div.p: THE RIXTON BRIDGE.

The4antllever bridge over the Rixton cutting is in a fair stage of advancement. On both sides of the canal, the ironwork is pushed out a considerable distance; and seems only to require the girder lying on five barges in the canal.to be place in position, and then the arch is complete. The scaffolding used by the riveton, &c., is strong and secure, and from the height of the bridge this had need to be. The bridge rests upon two piers built frombelow the bottom of the canal, andis kept in place by vertical, iron rods running the whole depth of the brick-work. The ends of the rods, with nuts at- tached, can he seen protruding above the iron bases of the arch. The bridge when complete will be•composed of a central arch and two halves. The central arch will ,cross the °canal, and the highest portion of the two 1 halves, as-seen now, rests upon the outer buttresses of the bridge. These buttresses have semi-circular flanks for the support of the tips which run with a curve from Liverpool-road to join with Newbridge-lane, before the lane crosses the river into Warburton. When 'finished, and open 'for traffic, it will be a stiff pull to surmount the bridge. The stonework in connection with the but- tresses is of,red sandstone, and the masons have been employed for-some time. The cutting is well filled with water

div.head: FTNANCIAL 'POSITION OF MANCHECTER.
div.p: THE FTNANCIAL 'POSITION OF MANCHECTER.

An adjourned special meeting of the Manchester City Council was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, The Mayor (Mr. Alderman Bosdin T. Leech) presided. The Mayor, on taking the chair, made the following state- ment:—Since our last Council meeting I lurre had 'many inquiries as to the-effect of the Ship Canal loan upon our rates, and I &Size to take the first opportunity of giving the following authoritative figures. lin the first place it is manifest that so long as we borrow suoney at 3i per cent.and the Ship Canal Company continue to pay us 4i per cent, no increase in the rates can possibly arise. Ti we leek at the case in the worst possible light, and assume that the Canal Company will cease to ,pay us any interest en the £3,0C13,000 lent, what would be the result ? The,cost to the Corporation for interest, stamp duty, manarr.,ement charges, kc., will be £98340 per annum for the £3,000,000., and as the actual yield of a rate of a penny ladle pound ie. nearly £ll,OOO, it will be seen that eupposing no interest at all were paid by the Ship Canal Company., the charge on the rates would be about Bd. in the pound. On the Ist January, 1895, a sinking fund oil per ;cent, is required to he set aside, and this would involve a further charge of :3d. in the pound, or a total for ,principal and interest of is. in the pound, and io 47 years the debt would be extinguished. In other words, each million borrowed may cost 4d. in the pound for principaland interest, and this charge will decrease as the rateable ralue increases. As regards the rates, it is no doubt correct that owing to the large and vet unremunerative works the Corporation are engaged in they have increased considerably during the last two years. but we still compare very favourably with other, I large towns. In the townskip of Manchester the total , rate last year was 4s. 61. in the pound: now it is ss. in'

div.head: lIA.YDOCK- COLLIERY DISASTER. INQUEST AND VERDICT.
div.p: THE lIA.YDOCK- COLLIERY DISASTER. INQUEST AND VERDICT.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, on Monday re- sumed his inquiry at the Waggon and. Horses Hotel. Haydock, into the circumstances attending the deaths A f Thos. Sharrock, Peter Cooke, and Thos. Ball, manager, fireman, and collier respectively,whe were suffocated by gas in the Southport mine, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Litnite 1, on Monday morning week. Mr. Henry Hall, Government inspector of mines, and Mr. D. IL P. Matthews, assistant Government inspector were present__

The firm of Messrs. R. Evans and Co. were repro- tented by Mr. T. R. Ellis, solicitor, Wigan ; Mr. J. Iligson, consulting engineer, Mr. S. Robinson, chief mining engineer and general agent of the collieries, and Mr. El. Squires, a director. The miners were represented by Mr. S. Woods, M.P., and Mr. T. Aspinall. Mr. Robinson handed to the coroner a qet of duplicate plans showing the situation of No. 4 and 5 pits and the site of the accident. These proved to be of great service to the jury. Mr. Robinson was the first witness called. Re said No. 4 pit was 510 yards deep, and the place where the men came by their deaths was about 120 yards from the shaft. Ventilation at the face of the coal was produced by a 20-inch air pipe down the shaft, and continued in 18-inch pipes, and by bratticing. Thomas Sharrock was the certificated manager,

- By Mr. Woods, M.P. : This particular place has been stopped from twelve o'clock on Saturday to six o'clock on Monday morning. Gas was reported, and it was in the report, but he did not know of it until after the accident. Sharrock was a competent man, and had practically conducted the sinking operations down to the °resent position. William Smales, fireman, said he had been a fireman under this firm for two years and six months, and had been assistant fireman at Pemberton previously, lie went down to the pit at a quarter-past five o'clock on Monday to see if there was any accumulation of gas, and if it was safe generally. He found two places safe, and then at a few minutes to six went into Ball's place. He came out to the pit shaft and knocked to be drawn up. At the top he saw Ball, who asked how his place was. Witness replied that there was gas at the top of his brow and he must not go until Peter Cooke had been up to examine it. Several other men named Tobin, Donavan, Johnson, and he believed M'Guire and Jackson were there when he told this to Ball, and they would hear it.
The Coroner here examined the report book, and found an entry. September 3.1 "A. little gas in Ell's brow through pipes being off." That, witness said, was

ten as soon as he came up. By the Coroner: He did not consider he had done everything that was required to do by Act of Parlia- ment. Mr. Oriman,analytical chemist, Gathurst,near Wigan, stated that two days after the accident he went to the working place and took samples of air—one from half- way between the face of the warrant and that of the coal. His analysis showed that to every one part of air there were two parts of gas. Looking at this it was easy to account for the rapid suffocation of the three men, as with so small a percentage of oxygen—only six per cent. instead of twenty per cent.—it would be al- most impossible for a man to live longer than a minute. James Tobin, who first missed the men and raised the alarm, and during his heroic efforts to help was rendered unconscious, was complimented by the Coroner. Witness said he heard Emales tell Ball there was gas in his place. —Thomas Donovan also confirmed this statement. Mr. Thomas Turner, underlooker, and Mr. James Seddon,manager, of neighbouring pits,who were fetched, , and who made every effort to reach the bodies promptly, also gave evidence. Mr. John Higson, mining engineer, said he was the consulting engineer to Mr. Richard Evans and Co. He made an examination of these workings on Friday last. He came to the conclusion that the ventilation at the momont was totally inadequate to deal with that feeder (the inrush of gas), which was unusual in its density and volume. He suspected, though he could not prove it, that there was no carbonic oxide but only fire damp. Had there been carbonic oxide the men would have been immediately poisoned. They had all under-estimated the density of the atmo- sphere they went into. In witness's opinion it was an error of 3udginent on the part of Cooke, and the other two would not do anything else but try to fetch him out. He never remembered a similar case in his thirty years'

experieneii; " , Mr. Hall, Government Inspector at Mines, said he went to the colliery on the day following the accident, and examined all the workings. On that particular side he found the ventilation generally in a sluggish condition, and the" return" from both sides showing caps of gas, The place was then full of gas, and apparently just the same as on the previous day, when the men were lost. He came to the conclusion that two things had led up to the disaster. First, the removal of the pipes, which bad interfered with the ventilation at the face; and the weak ventilation generally, which would have the effect of causing the gas when it did collect to be more deadly. He further thought that the fence not having been put up by the night fireman Might cause the men to consider it a smaller matter than it really was. But he was satis- fied that all the men knew before they went in that there was gas, and he thought the explanation of their going in was that they mistook its quality, and did not expect it to be of such a deadly character. In reply to Mr. S. Woods, the Government Inspoctor said he had no objection to the report book being kept on the top, providing it was in a place where men could I see it. They could perhaps, read it better in daylight, than below. In this instance the pit had not yet been laid out. He (Mr. Hall) knew Sharrock, and always thought he was a cautious man. He evidently rushed in to try and save the man Cook. The Coroner having summed up, the jury returned for half-an-hour, and then returned as their verdict " That the deceased came to their death, from suffocation from ; misadventure, being deceived as to the density .of the :.as." In reply to the Coroner, the foreman of tike jury limid that was the full verdict, and in their opinion there !aria no negligence on the part of Smales. The inquiry lasted nearly five hours.

div.head: EUROPE'S DUMPING GROUND.
div.p: EUROPE'S DUMPING GROUND.
BY H. WHITHAM.

I have been asked by ..s;;;;;I-Correspondents for a little further information touching the labour dis- putes now 80 much se evidence in the States. lam not quite clear as to my fitness to write upon this questiou. I fear that I have almost become, what the Americans call a" crank" upon the labour ques- tion. In my last letter,' hinted at the possibility of my saying something anent the Homestead strike. Since then strikes of more serious import, or at least with graver results, have occurred. Some of these strikes, as the one in Tennessee, are not of recent origin, but have been slumbering for months, biding their time, and,as opportunity offered, burst- ing out into wild fury. I feel very much like moral- izing, right away, before I even begin the miserable tale, and I fear, before I end this letter I shall tire the reader. If I had a nice house, all my own, some twenty, or thirty dollars a week coming in, or, say I bad a snug post on some paper, with orders to write " Up with protection "and "Down with the strikers," I think it possible my mind and pen would become as accustomed to slinging ink at the wage earner, and cringing before the wage- earners' owner as is the mind and pen of the usual writer of the daily press. No and again 1 come across a paper having a good word, and some good advice for the workers. I look for its politics, and surely.' find it Democratic. I also line that the Republican, or protectionist papers immediately poukce upon aubh, and denounce them as breeders of ' Anarchy and suggestors of dynamite. It ill accords with

PROTECTIONIST IDEAS that in this land of all the liberties there should be either. distress among the people, or the faintest , whisper of starvation wages being paid. American workers have yet to learn, what workers in Eng- land learnt long yeera ago.how to use the Press,how to call public opinion to their aid. They allow the newspaper fiend to interview them, and remain satisfied with a garbled report out of which capital can always be made by their enemies. It has re- cently been said in this city, by a clergyman who is labouring hard to break down race, class, and reli- gious prejudice,that the English workman is better educated than the American workman. That this is so I have not the least doubt, and I ascribe the fact, not so much to his school learning, as to his access to the best literature the world produces, in the leader columns of the dailies, and in the re- views. As I have said before,the English workman is solving slowly, yet surely, the labour problem. Every large city in England, and I must say almost every small town, has its east ends, towards which gravitate the sodden "drunks," the luckless poor, and the pauper aliens. These districts, in all cases, abound in drinking saloons where Solomon's advice to the "heavy hearts" is too well carried out, "Let him drink and forget his poverty,and remember his misery no more.' Outside of these cesspools of humanity, England can boast of as law-abiding and Irespectable and well-to-do working-class as can be found anywhere else in the civilized world. Leaving Free Trade England, skip France with her mode- rately sensible land laws, and enter Belgium; and here, looking at the proletarians in their unhappy surroundings, we may take in the whole of the European continent Germany, with its surging, restless, workers, ground under the heel of a royal despot, led by philosophical Socialists, who are al- ways in a state of chronic warfare with the powers that be,and protected to death by insane laws. Take in Spain and Italy,with a working-class population so densely ignorant as to call down the condemna- tion of the whole thinking world upon a church that has neglected its duty. Passing Into Russia, we find the whole of the preceding conditions in- tensified : a rich and selfish nobility, with a starved, I sickened, and superstitious peasantry; a student class fretting in its chains; a constant religious persecution always going on; a forced exodus urged on the most industrious portion of her people. Tak- ing a hasty view at all these EIIROPEAN FEATURES OF ThIE LABOUR QUESTION, we cannot wonder at the heading affixed to this letter. Yes, America is the dumping ground of Europe, a sort of cave of Adullam, where everyone who is in distress,and everyoue,who is discontented has hitherto freely entered in. A change has come over the spirit of the native American, and he no longer wishes this thing to go on. This cannot be wondered at,when it is known that within a month 1,000 Jews, refugees from Russia, have passed through Paris on their way to the United States. "Those who have recently arrived here have been in a most filthy condition. The places where they passed the nights were made so dirty by their occupation that it was found necessary to I thoroughly disinfect the premises after they had left." I have thought it necessary to say so much in order that readers may understand the position, at least as well as I may be thought to do. How [serious the case for America is may be seen from the statement of Dr. Gilman, who, referring to the continued necessity for .enlargement of lunatic asylums, says, " that the proportion of insane among the native population remains about the same; the increase comes from the wholesale im- portation a lunatics from central Europe." A very large proportion of the employers in the iron works, and other laborious trades in the States, are American mill,- in name, Europe has sent the good, the bad, and the indifferent, and America must, and will have to do the best she can with the medley, It would be no difficult matter to show that sTRIERS ARE ALWAYS ON ORDER, that at no time, so far this year, could it be said a strike was not on. The hands emeloyed at the Carnegie iron works, at Homestead, went on strike at midnight, June 24th. The difference was one- dol. between what was demanded by the strikers and what was offered by the Co. The scale of wages at the Carnegie mills expired by lapse of time June 24. The Co. offered a scale reducing the minimum rate for 4by 4 Bessemer billets from 2.5 dollars to 23 dollars. They also ordered the date of expiratidn of the scale—which is usually arranged for one year —to be changed from June 30 to December 31,with a reduction in tonnage rates in mills where im- proved machinery was used. The Co. offered to make it 24 dollars, but this was refused by the Amalgatnated Association of Iron and Steel Workers, on the ground that the selling price did not authorise the reduction. The Union stated that it had 50,000 dollars to spend, and it would spend it. The Co. said they did not propose to have the Union run their mills, and 80 the great Homestead strike began and the mills shut down. The strikers picketed the town against the non-union men, and ' took forcible possession of tie mills. The men offered arbitration,but this was refused. Two boat- loads of Pinkerton men arrived on the scene, but were refused a landing. Firing commenced. and several on both sides were killed. The Governor called out 8,500 militia men; three troops of cavalry and three batteries of artillery, and before the men I knew what was going to happen the troops had entered the town, which was at once placed under martial law. Non-union men were brought into the mills, which gradually began working. Things were going on moderately gently, when, on July 21, Mr. Frick was shot twice and stabbed several times by ' Anarchist Berkman of New York city. The day the news was brought of Mr. Prick's shooting, one of I the men in camp, Private Jams, called for three cheers for the men who s!iot, Frick% Jams refused I to take back his words, and was hung up by the thumbs, had his head half shaved, his whiskers half shaved, and was drummed out of the camp. The mills are now working, and Mr. Frick, who has covered, says he can hire more men than Ile such is a brief outline Ot

----• It was anticipated by both sides. The Company, had already placed their place in a state of defence. Electric apparatus was FO arrayed as to place a death-dealing power in their bands. I have seen no account of its use ; my opinion is, that from this strike dates a new era in America's labour troubles. We are now seeing the results of syndicates, and other criminial-combinatiOns." Ware fully realiz- ing what is meant by the saying and que,tion--, Cannot I do as I like with my own CatneAr IWtriipr'eSen't legiamate trade 4. represieftES monopoly, ponopoly of iron slepositg,,, ways, and water Ways.' The State has granted to him benefactions in way of special privileges, andi. he has grown hard, a many times millionaire. Ile poses in Scotland as a philanthropist. Many of his

workmen are living in houses they hoped some da to he their own. The Company holds mortgages on these homes to the ainount 0f.C30,000. These mort- gages will ti. foreclosed should new men go to work in the mils, and the old workmen's homes and investments will be lost. The presence in the land of powerful syndicates and trusts has practically reduced the wan who works to the level of a serf. nO matter what t:.e monopolist, or his apologist may Say to the contrary, and it is dollars against stoznachs, and dollars will win every time. Super- intendent Potter, of the Carnegie Company, stated that the plant was the finest in the world; the introduction of improved machinery increasing the amount of product and increasing the wages. Mr. Prick stated that the improved machinery had resulted in over production, hence the reduction offered. Senator Carlisle in a recent speech said— "The tendency towards a decline in the price of wages was, in his judgment, the necessary result of improved production ; two:of the strongest state- Meats ever put forward by exploiters of labour in favour of Socialist theories. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

-- The ordinary meetiug of this Bosrd was held on Tuesday afternoon. There were preeent Meisrs. T. C. Timmis (chairman), H. Wade Deacon, R. H. Davies, C. E. Harlow, and S. Quinn, Major Wareing, Dr. O'fieeffe, and Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk.

GENERAL PGRPOSNS COMAIITTRE. This committee's minutes containod the following item :—" To adopt. me report of the General Purposes Garnmittee with regard to the increase of salaries recom- mended by the School Management Committee:7—Th° report was adopted, on the motion of Mr. Deacon, seconded by the Chairman.

DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE, This committee submitted an abstract of figures, showing the work of the committee tor the yea ended August 31st, 1892, also reported that during th holiday, .the attendance officers had taken a censu . .

lof the" 'children of the district, the results of whic were now submitted to the Board in tabular form. —Mr. Deacon read, and commented on the abstract of educational work. He remarked that during the year there had been, in consequence of the passing of the Free Education Act, very few persons before the com- mittee, applying for payment ot fees, 247 having been the number as compared with 2,076 in 1891. The cases summoned before the committee, were 3,038 for 1892, compared with 4,180 in 1891, and the number of people for offences, had increased from 2,104, to 2,789. That increase, Mr. Deacon explained, was more apparent than real, because the committee found at the end of the year, that the old book in which these cases were recorded was full, and it was found so difficult to transfer the old cases into the new book, that it was determined to. start them in this as fresh cases. The prosecu— tions before the magistrates had fallen again— from 284 in 1891, to 245 in 1892. That was a., satisfactory feature. Only 2 children had been sea to industrial schools, a decrease of 3 from 1891, . and none had been sent to truant schools. The Board had now 20 children in the industrial schools, five fewer than in 1881. The average number of children on the rolls was 6,599 as compared with 6547.8 in 1891,. and the average attendance was better, 83.1 per cent. against 82.4 in 1891. This was all the greater improve- ment because the increase had been obtained with fewer prosecutions before the magistrates. This was the first year that the town had had the advantages of free education ; and the attendance was slightly better, but hardly anything to speak of, s ) that the freeing of schools had not, as far as it had gone, increased the , attendance. It was not thought that it would consider- ably increase it, because when the attendance got to a . very high figure it was always difficult to improve it.. Re would draw attention to the fact that the Inspector

was satisfied apparently with the work 'done. In that district. He quoted the following from Inspec- tor Phelps's report:—" Irregularity of attendance is un- doubtedly the greatest difficulty to be contended with. There is only one township in the district, Widnes,where I can say the attendance is really well looked after and enforced." It was satisfactory to have that reported by the inspector; it was also satisfactory to know that in Widnes they had no half timers; they did not permit it. Their standard of total exemption was also high,the 6th,, until a lad was thirteen. Altogether,ms tters were fairly satisfactory. One would like to have seen the attend- ance rather better, but it was evidently exceedingly difficult to get beyond about 85 per cent. A few years ago it was 85, now it was 83, and it was 82.4 in 1891.—The Chairman said the committee could not be blamed in this matter, and asked what was the average lat,endance for the United Kingdom.—The Clerk : 75.—Mr. Deacon then read and commented on the table of the results of the census of children. He pAnted out that the number of inhabited houses was now 5,269, an increase since the census, 2 years ago, of 130. The empty houses had in- creased by 24. The number of houses in course ot erec- tion was 41, an increase of 1. The total accommoda- tion was 7,284 ; having been 6,992, two years ago. The number of children between 3 and 13 was now 7,69(, an increase of 47, and making the usual deductions, there was an excess of accommodatron shown for 1,675 chil- dren. The return •V 15 very satisfactory. Thapnr.,,n. tion was evidently increasing very slowly, but it was steadily increasing, and it was to be hoped it would continue to do so. Mr. Deacon moved the adoption of ' the reports he had read, and, the Chairman having. secou&d, they were adopted accordingly.

div.head: SERIOUS AFFAIR AT A SuCTITPORT
div.p: SERIOUS AFFAIR AT A SuCTITPORT
HO TEL

At the Southport Police Court, on Friday morning, Archibald Colquhoun, a gentleman of no fired address, will be brought up in custody charged with shooting with inte.nd to kill. Prisoner, who had been staying for- several days at the Bold Arms Hotel, Southport, had my Thursday morning an altercation in the smokeroom with, Mr. Prescott Morris, a young gentleman of his acquaint- ance, who resides at Rock House, Upholland. The - quarrel, which, it is said, arose through jealousy, reached an acute stage, and Colquhoun, it is alleged, drew a six-chambered revolver, which he placed to the head of Morris and fired. Morris turned aside, bet the powder burned his cheek, the bullet passfidThrough the door, just missing a waiter, piercing a partition, and flattening against a wall. The " b-iots " rushed in and disarmed Colquhoun, who was received in custody by Detective- inspector Halsall and Police-constable Henderson (34). ['sisall took posses-ion of the revolver, which had five chambers still loaded. Before being taken to a cell the prisoner had a long interview with Mr. H. S. Threlfall,. solicitor, who took rrltes for his defence.

Licensing WARRINGTON 11219,1011 g been rnoted as at a drink-ridden town;: and,. s:clging Warrington. from the action of the majority of magistrates at the adjourned licensing session, on Thesday, it is likely to be drink-ridden fox years to come. We say the majority; for it is din:e to the !minority to state that they,at anyrate,are n.otto be used as catspaws for pulling somebodys.akestents out of the fire. For nearly a generation.th 3 policy pursued by the Bench has been to refusskapplica- tions for new licenses, on the ground that there are already far too many drink-shops, in the , town. Indeed, the fact is so glaring and the results aro so discreditable—especially as to Buttermarket-street—that complaints have , been numerous both frs4m tradespeople and the Chief Constable. So badihadmatters become that, three years ago, in what proves,to: have been ' a transient fit al virtue, the magistrate& drew up a rtport in which a considerable number licensed houses in the centre of thalown werealulieshiled as unsuitable, from one reason or anothen„ for the use Ito which they were put. Soon.aften• that it was decided by the highest COurts that the magistrates had absolute discretion in ref using to renew the licenses of such houses;-and-it NTP.Si then thought that the Licensing Juatices of I.Witurington would act upon the lines of their own report. But not so; if they had convictions, thew were lacking in courage; for since they wore. assured of their power, Ise report, safer as.theu are concerned, hack never been heard of. Can it be that Messrm. GREESAIL, Wilinzv, and have struck terms into their hearts because they have talked about appealing against any decision that might be givem against thain ? Gr. is it that the justices' idea of justice ia to give unto him that has much, and, in effect, take fresa Linn that has littla even that which he, has ? The big brawers of 'Warrington are indeealasati- able ; they toe owneraof the bulk of the kicensed houses in the borough ;but they are not satisfied. Like the Jaughtera of the horse-leech, their cry is still "Give, give" ;and the magistrates'," blind as never bat was blind" to the true interests of the town, have thrown two new districts into their ravenous maw. They have their excuse of course; for excuses are easily provide& They seek to justify themselves upon the ground that Messrs. GISEENALL, Winatny, and Co are giving up old licenses in congested districts in order to obtain these new licenses in new districts. Giving up indeed! What a farce this is 1 What a mockery of the relations which ought to exist between appli-

----- cants and magistrates! The magistrates grant privileges in the shape of licenses--privileges good for twelve months only ; and the holders of these privileges have the audacity to come into court and seek to barter with those who have granted these privileges as if they were rights; while the magistrates, either ignonint of the law„ or too. timid to apply the law, fall into the pit whicht has been dug for them in the sight of all men. Alderman CHANDLE:Y revealed this when he said " The inducements which have been, offered: to us, will enable us to reduce the number of licenses." If Alderman CLIANDSEY and his fellow magistrates had been equal to the occasion, they would have declined, to consider brewers' induce, merits to "reduce the number of licenses, they would have reduced them not out of regard to the, brewers interests but inthe interestsof the inhabi- tants.. They have the pewer—why have they failed to exercise it ? It is true that Mr. Robert DAVOS' said "there must be good judicial reasons for re-. fusing a license." Of course there must; but them are no more judicial reasons required for reftising to renew than for refusing a new license ; and nobody knows this better than Mr.. Robert, DAVIS. The magistrates have not only,.as Mr. CHOHLTON: showed, full authority, or absolute dis- cretion, in refusing renewals; but it is their (WY to exercise that power in congested districts. The wants to be considered are not the wants of brewers, but " the wants of the neighbourhooe Granting that it was for the justices to decide whether a full license was required in the Bowser' road and in the Battersby-lane districts, it a'aa surely of moment to them to know the wishes of the itiliabitantAes ;-. and as to this, as Alderman PUTT stated, the evidence is overwhelming that they do not want these new licensed houses in their midst. At present, those who suffer from drink - shops being thrust upon them are disregarded but there is some consolation in thinking, that the time is not far distant when the power which the magistrates exercise will be given to the peePl& themselves. Further, assuming that full licenser were needed, is it not in harmony alike vritll' common-sense and common fairness that this., should be accomplished—not by additional licenses • —but by enlarging existing licenses ?- Appliestll9/1' to this end has been made by the owners of "The', Grove" in Bewsoy-road for seventeen yea The magistrates have themselves, in the pasty admitted that this house hadthe first claim ; and yet in face' of this they not only 'refuse "The Grove," but go a long way towards ruining the h-use.by granting the full license to Messrs. GREENALLf. WHITLEYr• and Co., who have not as much as a stick or a` r 3,. , stone on the ground.. And so with regard to Councillar BoixoN ; ho is in possession of th:' Battersby-lane district with an off-license ;• and offers three licenses, or 'l,OOO, for the full license which is said to be needed. But the magistrates' turn a deaf ear to him ; they have no privileges to grant except to Messrs•GICEENALL, WHITLEY; and. Co., who are given the monopoly as full-license!i holders of two new districts;, and when this la' done the people of Warrington are expected to respect the transaction as a sample 0!. " equal and exact justice to all lie' regards BOLTON is an aggrieved man;' regards himself as robbed--robbed to the tune. of £l,ooo—the sum he offered in court for the privi- lege which has been given to his rivals.- The. owners and the occupiers of "The Grove" fra°,,e' spent a small fortune in • applications for ao license; and they, too, fool as though they. Were being robbed when that full license is , granted f another firm whose claim is scouted bY bulk of the residents of the district. The seal 6 it all is this—that the town, is being further', de- graded ; it is being again over-ridden by

is already a parting of the ways even amongst Politichlns who may be said to be in favour of an eight-I,oura day. It is obvious, therefore, that there is a great deal of ground to clear. What, to begin with, of trade option ? From the resolution *4lopted at the St. Helens meeting, it would ItPpear to mean that the ballot of a particular trade shall settle the question of working hours for the whole of that trade throughout the United Kingdom. On the other hand, in the "tree of the speeches, reference was made to " local " option in trade matters, which Would imply that a given trade in a given district toight have it left to them to fix their own hours. There is of course a wide difference between the two methods; and Sir CHARLES DILKE must have been thinking of this form of local option when he 4Poke of one district as possibly acting prejudi- &ly to another. For instance, if the masons of 'Llenehester adopted eight hours, whilst the mem- °ere ef the same trade in Liverpool continued to work nine hours,- it is a matter of course to say that the two cities would not be upon an equal fc":)ting in the matter of contracts and wages. This wouldn't work well for either employers or em- 131°Yed• A trade option which embraced all the members of a trade would not be unobjectionable, although less objectionable. What if joiners Were under the nine hours system, while plumbers Were subject to the eight-hours option ? We should then witness the spectacle of one class of builders workmen" knocking off" whilst another reutinued at work—an irregularity which would scl to confusion at times and interfere with pro- l'eBe. There is a "sweet simplicity" about Sir Fharics DICKE'S proposal to fix the hours of labour Irir the whole country at one time ; but would it W°tlr ? It, in its turn, raises new difficulties—diffi- etlties which will require much further considera- °la before it will be safe to act in the matter.

Mr. William Diggle is like the lady in the song who say, : -

" I will speak my mind if I die for it." He sees in the Watrington epidemic of scarlet fever and sarill-pox the results of neglect of the warnings he has oiven about the Depots and the night-soil vans. 'Ho has plans of his own for mending matters, and, as the Sanitary Com- mittee won't listen to him, he is going to see if the public will give him a hearing. He has engaged the Co-operative Hall, in Sankey-st., and intends to hold forth on " The Sanitary Condition of Warrington, and how to improve it," on Wednes- day night next, at 8 o'clock. Admission, like speech, is to be free ; but there will be a collection of pence (as well as ideas) " to defray expenses."

"There is a soul of good in things evil"—a truth which will receive illustration if it should happen that the scare amongst the "upper tea " about the risk they run from wearing garments made in sweating dens, should result in the dens being swept away. It is stated that the daughter of the late Sir Robert Peel caught the fever from which she died frora it riding habit which wos infected in the making ; ;1;A it is suggested that the late Duke of Clarence may have been it victim to the evil influence of a double-breasted coat which was altered,in a crowded workshop,by a tailor who was stricken, next day, with influenza.. The whole subject needs to be further ventilated, for there is disease and death in the air.

Subscriptions are being obtained for a memorial to James Thompson, the author of" The Seasons." The tribute to his memory is somewhat late, seeing that he died so far back as 1748. His blank verso is not much read now, but yet it contains some memorial lines such as : Come gentle Spring! ethereal mildness come !" and— _

Loveliness Needs not the foreign aid of ornament, But is, when unadorned. adorned the most. The poet wrote, too, a poem called" The Castle of Indolence"; and it is understood that, as an easy- going fellow, he introduced no little personal experience. One satirist thus hits him off:— Thompson who sung about the" Seasons " said It was a glorious thing to rise in season ; But then he said it lying,—in his bed— At ten a.m.—the very reason He wrote so charmingly ; the simple fact is His preaching was'nt sanctioned by his practice.

About half-past four on Monday afternoon, a boy had a narrow escape from meeting with very serious injuries. He was riding in a cart laden with empty boxes, and when opposite Devonshire-buildings he fell off, and but for the prompt manner in which the driver pulled up, his legs would have been run over, they being within an inch or two of the wheel when the vehicle was brought to a standstill. As it was, the little fellow was badly stunnPd by the fall, but after receiving careful attention at the hands of Mr. Weston, druggist, he appeared little the worse for the mishap. div.head: SINGULAR ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SINGULAR ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

On Monday afternocn, about half-past two, a some- what serious accident betel the daughter of Mr. Rowles, landlord of the Duke of Edinburgh, in Davonshire- square, Runcorn, under the following circumstances. She was handling a bottle of aerated waters, when it burst, and a piece of class caught her on the left side of the neck, inflicting a very ugly wound. She was promptly attended by Dr. McKenzie. If the injury had been an eighth of an inch higher, the case might have proved serious, as one of the principal arteries would have been severed, from which she might have speedily bled to death.
