At the Widnes Police Court,on Monday, before Messrs. H. Wade Deacon and F. A. St.apleton liretherton, James Muiray, farm labourer, nom, was charged with stealing L 163. Sd.,the property of Martin Carr. Prosecutor said he slept In the same room as prisoner, at a farm in Bold, and on Saturday night,as is was going to bed,his money dropped out of his pocket. He picked it up, and put it in his trousers pocket again,and went to bed. When he got up next morning, the money was gone. Witness asked prisoner if he knew where it was, but lie said lie did not. P.C. Forster was subsequently sent for, and prisoner told him he had put the money under a step near the granary. The officer looked in the place indi- cated, and found the money wrapped in a handkerchief, which prosecutor identified. Prisoner pleaded guilty.— A fine of 305., or 14 days in default, was imposed.

div.head: AGGRAVATED ASSAULT AT RUNCORN,
div.p: AGGRAVATED ASSAULT AT RUNCORN,

Oa Thursday morning, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. J. Brundrit and O. L. Davies, a man named John Atkin was brought up under a warrant charged with committing an aggravated assault on Matthew James Smith, a labourer, employed on the Manchester Ship Canal, and residing in Norfolk-st., Runcorn, on Tuesday last. From the evidence it ap- peared that the prisoner's brother and his wife had been lodging with the prosecutor a.bont three weeks, and on the morning of the day in question they told Smith not to admit the prisoner to the house, but later on the same day they came with the prisoner to the house. Prosecu- tor refused Atkin admission, whereupon they flashed him to the ground, and the prisoner attacked him with a stick. The prosecutor managed to get on the top .f Atkin on the ground, and while in that position prisoner deliberately kicked him in the face with the heavy boots he was wearing at the time. The result of the kick was that the skin was torn off one of his cheeks, causing a very serious injury. The magistrates sent the prisoner to gaol for two months with hard labour.
ALLEGED UNPROVOKED BRUTAL ASSAULT AT WIDNES.

. On Saturday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, Richard Taylor, Witt-road, was charged with unlawfully wounding Mr. Eli Steinhardt, painter, &c.. Alforde-st., by kicking him on the leg. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. It was stated that on Friday night the prosecutor was in company with Mr. J.Davies, house agent, about eleven o'clock, near the London and North-Western railway station, Widnes, when prisoner came up and spoke to them. The prosecutor told him he did not want anything to do with him, and walked away. Prisoner followed, and was again requested to go away, whereupon he struck Mr. Steinhardt in his face, and afterwards knocked him down, kicked him on the ankle, and then fell on the top of him. Dr. Mc Cambridge stated that one bone in prosecutor's left ankle was broken, and another dislocated. He would be unable to appear in court for three or four weeks,and it would be three months before he would be able to walk without the aid of crutches.—The police replied for a remand for eight days; which was granted, and on the application of Mr. Knowles, prisoner was admitted to hail.

div.head: SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES AT RUNCORN.

The Science and Art Committee have issued an excel- lent programme of classes. Not many new subjects have been introduced, but some of those previously taught are to have more time devoted to them, and to be taught with greater thoroughness. The art classes will be under the direction of Mr. J. B. Gibbs, artist, of 33, Bold-st., Liverpool. He is an art master, and one or two of his painting,s find a place in the Autumn Exhibition at Liverpool The machine construction and building classes will be taught separately, the fernier by Mr. John Speakman, draughtsman at Messrs. Timmin's en. gineering works, and the latter by Mr. J. Wilding, who, since he undertook the class, has been appointed assistant : surveyor to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Mr. B. Crosby, who last year taught electricity, and ; sound, light and heat with much success, will this year have to additional classes, one in physiography and one in theoretical chemistry. Another new class in applied mechanics will be conducted by Mr. B. Davies, an accom- plished science teacher, of Warrington. It may be added that these classes will have the advantage of using the excellent collection of mo leis and apparatus which has lately been purchased. Mons. Meunier will resume his French class, and Mr. Whalley will teach shorthand. The dressmaking class, which was found to be much appreciated last season, will be resumed, and last, but not least in importance, cooking will find a place in the arrangements.

HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN. The thanksgiving services in connection with the ingathering of the harvest were commenced at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Thursday evening. The sacred edifice presented a very pleasing appearance, it being prettily adorned by the tollowing ladies :—The Misses Preston, Mesdames Riley, Willin, and Harrison, and the Misses Fisher, Wells, Tyrie, Gough, and Stubbs. They were greatly assisted by the Rev. A. Riley. Plants and flowers were kindly contribired by Mr. S. B. Chad- wick, J.P., of Crofton Lodge, Runcorn; a quantity of choice blooms came from Mrs. Moon. London ; and other decorative material was kindly forwarded by Mrs. Haziehurst, Mrs. IVillin, Mrs. Harrison, Miss Tyrie, Mrs. Savage, Messrs. Ackerley, Roberts, Salkeld, Mrs. Horse- field, Mr. Waterworth, Miss Coleburn, Mrs. Marsh. Mrs. Meadowcroft, and other friends. The preacher on Thursday evening was the Rev. W. RusCoRN FREE LIBRARY. The usual monthly meeting of the Free Public Library Committee was held in the Board-room, Town Hall, on ‘Vednesday. There were present—Mr. J. Simpson, Mr. W. Handley, Mr. W. Leach, Dr. Mangan, and Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian). The Librarian read the names of the committee appointed by the Commissioners at their meeting on September Bth, and on the motion of Mr. Simpson, seconded by Dr. Mangan, Mr. Thomas Riley was re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Win. Handley was then voted to the chair in the absence of Mr. Riley. Mr. Leach moved. and Dr. Mangan seconded, a resolution that Mr. William Handley be the vice-chairman for the ensuing year, which was carried.- The Book Selection Committee, consisting of all the tnembers of the Library Committee, was reappointed. It was resolved that the meetings of the committee be held on the third Wednesday in the month, at 10.30 a.m. The Librarian reported that during August 1,752 works had been issued from the library. A list containing 125 volumes of new books was submitted by the Book Selec- tion Committee, and recommended to be purchased. Various gifts were received during the month.
RUNCORN WATER WORKS, AND THE SUPPLY TO THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY.

A meeting of the shareholders of the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Waterworks Company was held on Monday afternoon, at their offices, the Public Hall, Runcorn. There were present Mr. J. Brundrit (chairman), Mr. Hayes, Mr. Simpson, Mr. Whittaker, Mr. Salkeld (secre- tary), and Mr. J. Ashton (solicitor to the company). There were also in attendance, and by proxy, more than three-fourths of the value of the company and the number of shareholders. The Secretary read the notice convening the meeting, after which the Chairman stated in general terms the object of their beingcalled together. Mr. Ashton then read a draft agreement between the company, the Corporation of Liverpool, and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, whic's was to tlse effect that the latter agreed to pay a royalty of 2d. per thousand gallons to the Water Works Company for all water used by them from the mains of the Liverpool supply, at Norton, to their works in the company's dis- trict. On the motion of Mr. Hayes, seconded by Mr. Simpson, it was unanimously resolved that the agree- ment be adopted. ALLEGED HIGHWXY ROBBERY BY BOYS. On Tuesday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, four boys, named John Fitzsimons,7, Duke-st., Ditton ; Thomas McDermott, 10, Duke-tit. ; Charles Smith, 11, Duke-st. ; and Sam Sterrett, Wood's Cottage. Ditton, were charged with stealing 31. from the person of Henry Redfern, and a ld. from the per- son of Fred. Redfern. Henry Redfern (131, residing with his parents at 5, Waterloo-road, stated that about half-past six on Saturday night he was going with his brother down Ditton Brook path when they met the four prisoners. Fitzsimons asked witness for some mosey. He told him he had none, and walked on, but in a few minutes he put 31 from his Waistcoat pocket into his trousers pocket. Fitzsimons then ran up, caught hold of him, turned his pockets out, and took 3d., but when he was coming back Sterrett gave him 2d. back. Wit- ness saw McDermott and Smith get hold of his brother's legs and turn him up, and take something from his pockets. He was certain the four prisoners were the same lads. Frederick Reefern (14), brother of the last witness corroborated. The prisoners, who were re- :nanded on Tuesday, were brought up at the Petty Ses- sions on Thursday, but aS there was only one magistrate present, the case was adjourned until Monday. div.head: TUB PARAFFIN LAMP FATAL/Ty AT PARR.
div.p: TUB PARAFFIN LAMP FATAL/Ty AT PARR.

Mrs. Esther Greener, aged forty-six years, of Merton Bank-road, Parr, St. Helens, who was so severely burned on the 2nd inst. by the upsetting of a paraffin lamp in her house, succumbed to her injuries on Saturday. It will be remembered that a child named Henry Daniels,of Sutton, whilst on a visit to a house in Merton Bank-road, strayed into the back portion occupied by Mrs. Greener, and while there pulled over a paraffin lamp. The child died a few days afterwards. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens, on Tuesday. The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidental death."

- MIGRATION OF LANCASHIRE FARMERS TO ESSEX.

A colony of Lancashire farmers, was founded in Essex a few years ago alongside the Scotch colony in that county. Another migration of the same kind is about to be made. At midnight on Sunday a batch of farmers frost North Lancashire stated for Essex to spy out the land. In Essex rents are very low indeed. Heavy land can be bought for .£lO or .£l2 per acre ; and it is stated that a large farm has been offered to one of the migrants at 7s. 61. per acre. Under these circumstances, and as London is hard by, and barge manure is delivered at 31. 6d. per ton, the enterprise is not «levoid of hopeful prospects. liovsKnoLD LINENS hemmed and marked free of charge.— Land W. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

About half-past seven on Saturday morning an accident occurred at St. Helens Railway Station. A mineral train from Clock Face to St. Helens entered the station at a good speed, and was being turned into the loop line under Sharp-st. bridge, when live or six waggons left the rails. The following aggons crasl)o into them and knocked the dis- placed waggons across both main lines. Some of the waggons were badly damaged. A staff of men set to work under the instruction of Mr. Henry Fartington, acting stationmaster for Mr. Boardman, who was away on his holidays, and the obstruction was cleared as rapidly as possible. One or two passenger trains were delayed for half an hour.
THE PROPOSED TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS IN RUNCORN
UNION.

The poll of the ratepayers' of the Runcorn Union as to whether they are in favour of the elections of Guardians being triennial has been taken this week. The voting papers were distributed on Thursday and collected yesterday. The counting will begin to day at Dutton Workhouse, though it is possible the result may, not he known till Monday.

With the exception of the steel-rail branch, there has been no notable addition to the orders received in any of the various departments of the English iron and steel trades. Bath pig and manufactured iron exhibit little vitality, and lower prices rule for the 'latter. In steel generally little is doing, but in the north-west the Barrow Hematite Steel Co. has received orders foi nearly 26,000 tons of rails during the past week. Shipbuilders and engineers are quiet. The coal trade shows fair movement.— Iron. UMBRELLAS 12F.COVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adr. Alit. P. J. KING AND SIR CHARLES DILKE.

In consequence of a stateineiit made by Sir Charles Dilke at the St. Helens t rsiles demonstra- tion on Saturday to the effect that the St. Helens evidence before the Royal Labour Commissi,n led him to conclude that the only subject that appeared to occupy the minds of t4l e local labour leaders was how to contract out of the Employers' Liability Act, Mr. I'. J. King, president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, who adduced evidence on the necessity of an eight hours day and other matters, wrote and called his attention to the fact. Sir Charles Mike, writing from Merthyr on Wed- nesday, says :—" If I used the words you quote they were too wide. I was at the time speaking of the miners, and the miners only. With regret that I should have caused you trouble, sincerely yours, Charles alke." AGRICULTURAL TRAINING IN LANCASHIRE.

At a meeting of the Liverpool District Farmers' Club, held on Saturday, it was stated that the com- mittee appointed to deal with the suggested farm schools had forwarded to the Lanett:o6re County Council a series of suggestions. embodying what the committee considered a practicable plan for the promotion of agricultural training as a part of the technical instruction scheme of the Council. The suggestions included the following:—That the West Derby Hundred be arranged in divisions, and that the present unions—namely, Ormskirk, Prescot, Wigan, and part of Warrington—be taken as those divisions ; that arrangements be made for the train- ing of boys ti tid girls in suitable branches of farm- ing upon some farm or farms situated as near as possible in the centre of each union, where mixed husbandry is or may be conveniently practised, and that such farms shall not be taken out of the hands of their occupiers, who will still remain the tenants, and will continue to prsvide all stock, implements, seeds, manures, &c., and be the owners of all the products of the tarms ; that the tenants of such farms shall be paid an annual stipend, for which they shall undertake the general control of the pupils, shall adiait them into the operations of the farm,and instruct them in the practical use of 11l implements, as well as in all actual manual labour; that a committee of inspec- tion be appointed by the County Council for the purpose of visiting the school farms and securing the proper carrying out of the object of the scheme, which is—that the youth of the county shall be in- structed in the correct principles of the science of agriculture, and in the most approved and efficient methods of its practice.

div.head: WARRINGTON WHITE STAR MINSCIIIILS.
div.p: WARRINGTON WHITE STAR MINSCIIIILS.

On Monday evening this troupe of minstrels opened their second season by giving a performance in the Public Hall, Runcorn, in aid of St. John the Baptist Schools, Weston. Norwithstanding the somewhat inclement weather there was a very fair at tendance,atzongst the audience being the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi and Canon Clegge,of Neston,and the success of the proceedings depended in no small manner on the former gentleman's un, iring exertions. Mr. J. Wright was the interlocutor. The opening chorus, "Down the River," was very creditably given by the troupe. Mr. a Newton effectually rendered " Lore's old song." Much amusement was caused by Mr. Coggins's " Razors in the air," and Mr. J. Fury was warmly applauded for "The Old Sexton." " The old folks at home " was nicely sung by Mr. a Houghton. "My Gal," by Mr. 11. Skidmore, was a decided feature in the performance, and it was received with due appreciation. "Only to see her face '• was well sung ' by Mr. Hassid!. Mr. J. Emson, in his " Mar's gone with a coon." was quite at home, and "Clare Nolan's Ball." by Mr. J. P. McDonald, was well received. Mr. D'Alton was in fine voice for " Eileen Alannah." " Marching through Georgia" brough: tie first part to a close. It may be said that the choruses throughout were given very fully and evenly, and ' reflect much cradit upon the musical conductor and pianist, Mr. G. Riley. The second part opened with a piccolo solo by Mr. Morgan, given in a masterly manner, and Messrs. Morgan and Rowley's perform- ance with the piccolo and bones was loudly applauded. Mr. 11. Skidmore gave "After me" in fine style, and received an enthusiastic encore, when he sang " Give her my kind regards." "The Mulligan Guards " was the cause of much amuse- ment. A comic sketch " Advertising for a com- pany," was decidedly good, and much enjoyed.

div.head: POACHING NE kit RUNCORN.
div.p: POACHING NE kit RUNCORN.
A MIDNIGHr STRUGGLE.

On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Messrs. J. Brund rit and C. Reynolds, Charles Stubbs, sen., Charles Stubbs, jun., and William Stubbs, were charged on remand with unlawfully taking and destroying 15 rabbits on land belonging to Sir Richard Marcus Brooke, Bart., at 11.30 on Friday night, at Stockham. They were also charged with assaultiag William Knight and George Rigby, game- keepers. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys prosecuted. The prisoners admitted the offence with regard to poaching. Mr. Humphreys, in stating the case, said so long as the prisoners had admitted one offence he would briefly put before the Bench the facts and then call evidence in proof of the assault. About 11.30 on Friday night six keepers of Sir Richard Marcus Brooke, Bart., were on duty hi Gorse Wood, near Stockhain. It was a starry night, and they saw the three prisoners and four other; coming along setting nets. The keepers left their hiding- place, and on being seen the men called out, "Heigh, up, chaps, come on," which was followed by a shower of stones, and when they closed in sticks were freely used. Rigby got his arm badly hurt and Knight re- ceived a severe cut on the head, as well as an injury by a stone on the arm. Another keeper named Jones was also cut about the hands and hit upon the breast. He suggested, however, that they be only charged with assaulting Knight and Rigby. Without exception the men had implements upon them. they had all sticks and close by were found 15 rabbits in swarm condition showing that they had been recently killed. With regard to the assault, although William Stubbs did the actual violence, the law held that inasmuch as they all took part in the affray they were guilty of the assault. The other four or five men got away. When the prisoners were brought to the Police Statien, and charged with the offence, they made no remark. Stubbs, sen., had a stone in his pocket, and the sons too. He asked the Bench to inflict such a penalty, if the case were proved, that would deter the men before thein,as well as others, from again committing such an offence. George Rigby. gamekeeper, deposed that on Friday night, at 11.30, he and five other keepers were engaged in Gorse Wood, when they saw seven or eight men setting nets. On leaving their hiding-place the men pelted diem with stones, and on getting into close quarters they struck them with sticks. His arm was badly hruised. William Knight gave corroborative evidence,and stated that William Stubbs struck him on the head with a stick thereby causing a severe wound which had been attended.—By the elder prisoner: They were not the ground together for ten minutes. He did not ask for mercy, nor did he scream murder, nmi did he beg of them not to kill him.

Albert West stated that whilst putting the handcuffs on Charles Stubbs, his son William came up and struck him across the head and shoulders. The father threw a stone at him, after which they closed, fell down together and strunled for some time. In answer to the charge, Charles Stubbs, seri., said hs he Iliad been half kilkal, and ha contended that the keepers were the first to commence the fight. He was very sorry, and asked for lenient treatment. Charles Stubbs, junior. 6ta ted that he had never hit anyone, but was hit himself. William Stubbs asked the Bench to be merci- ful.

• The two Charles Stubbs were each fined ttas. and 7s. 6d. ccsts, or one nvintlC3 impri3onment for the poaching offence; and a fine of 4.05. and 6s. costs each was imposed for the assault, or a further term of a month's!nearceration. The implements seized were to be confiscated.

Another terrible disaster has occurred at Shreve, Ohin, a passenger and goods train coming into collision, with the result that nine persons were killed and five injured. The British brig Ephratah has gone ashore at Adicora and is a total loss. The crew have been landed at Curacoa. It is feared that the Liverpool barque Royal Arch. from Cardiff for Buenos Ayres, has been lost with all on board.

ELECTION AT WIDNES.
sELEcnos OF THE LIBERAL CANDIDATES.

A meeting of the Liberal Two Hundred of the Widnes Division Liberal Association was hehl on Wednesday evening, in the Lscey-streec School- room, under the presidency of Mr. E. Casey. There was a large att endance,the business being the selec- tion of candidates for the approaching municipal election-Ttlie first in the newly-created borough of Widnes. The proceedings were conducted in pri- vate, but it is stated, however, that the following is an accurate summary of the proceedings :—lt was decided that the party should at the first meeting of the Council on November 9th support the election of Mr.F. 11. Gossage (chairman of the present Local Board and the Provisional Mayor) as one of the six aldermen,and also as the first Mayor of the borough. The total strength of the (homed will be twenty-four —six aldermen and IS couzictllors. It was after- wards decided not to contest the Furnworth Warn, but to run cart.lidateA tor the other fire wards— West Rank, Waterloo, Victoria, Situtn's Cross and Halton—and also to support seven cAn.tidates selected by the Irish Nattoi.al League: ‘v hen the compact was entered into bet We 1i the two parties some time ago, it. Was aw.reett to allot ,event seats to the NATionaliStS, Toe meeting afterwattla resolved to run eight caihlidates at the tir..4 election on the Ist cit November, and on tile ninth of toe same month the elected Liberal nnlinbers are to en- deavour to place three of their number on the aldermaine bench, which woull create, of course, three Liberal vacancies. Wednesday night's meeting was called to select the eleven g.ettle- men, and the election was by ballot, the first eight so stand in the first nstance for election as councillors, and the next three for the vacancies created by the election of alderman on the 9th of November. The ballot paper contained the names of the following fifteen gentlemen :—Major Ware- ing, Messrs. W. W. Gossage, E. F. Gossage, H. S. Timmis, H. B. Shores (Liberal secretary), W. llodg- kinson. S. Owens, I'. Smith, J. Midwood, E. Manley S. Sadler, R. Roberts, J. Handley, G. Davies, and J. Houghton. Messrs. It. Roberts and T. Smith with- drew their names, so that there were thirteen gen- tlemen for the eleven appointments. The voting resulted in the gentlemen being seleete4 i the fol- lowing order :—Mr. H. B. Shores, Major Wareing, Messrs. S. Owens, S. Sadler, J. Midwood, W. W. Gossage, 11. S. Timmis, W. Ilodgkinson, E. F. Gos- sage, J. Handley, and (3. Davies. Mr. Shores, having received the largest number of votes, has the first choice of the ward be will stand for, and so on in the order named above to the eleventh. Messrs. Owens, Sadler, Midwood, and Timmis are members of the present Local Board, as is also Mr. J. Hough- , ton who was voted out.

The Nationalists have held several meetings to consider the matter, but up to the present the names of their seven candidates have not been made public. The names of Messrs. 11. Singleton, T. Carroll, 11. O'Donnell, and T. Williamson are, how- ever, freely mentioned as likely nominees of the party. The Conservative party have not yet taken any action. Should no independent candidates come forward, three of their nominees will have a walk- over in larnworth Ward, but it is generally felt that they should contest several other seats, al- though they will have the combined forces of Liberals and Nationalists against them. The Ratepayers' Association, it is stateiLare con- sidering the advisability of bringing forward can- didates, and it is more than likely that several " independents" will enter the field, the first niuni- cipal election in Widnes promises to be au interest- ing and exciting one.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT FROM A SHOP AT
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT FROM A SHOP AT
RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. Brundrit, Wm. Jones and John Perry were charged with breaking and entering the shop of Thomas Whinyates, boot and shoe dealer, Church- street, between 10 p.m. on the 13th, and 6 a.m. on the 14th September, and stealing six pairs of boots belonging to Mr. Whinyates, and three knives, book, an apron, a bass, a brush, and a pair of slippers, the property of Edward Chatterten.— Samuel Whinyatea deposed to leaving the premises securely fastened at 9.50 on Tuesday night. On going to the premises at six o'clock on the following morning, he found a pane of glass in the workshop window had been broken, and an entrance effected. On going into the shop he missed the whole of the articles.—P.S. Cheeney, of Warrington, said he appre- hended the prisoners in that town about 5 p.m. on Sep- tember 14th. He received three pairs of boors from the second-hand shop kept by Mrs. Leslie, in Mersey-at., Warrington.—P.C. tfregory received the prisoners into custody from the Warrington police. On bringing them to Runcorn he charged them with the offence, but did not receive a reply.. In the train Jones told him he visited Runcorn for the purpose of breaking into Mr. Whinyates' shop. Prom information received from Jones he went to Moore, where he found three pairs of boots at the spot named by the prisoner. Jones had nothing to say in answer to the chatge,but Perry stated that he met his fellow-prisoner on the 14th inst., and in accordance with his wish he referred him to a lodging-house. He also showed him three pawnshops. He accompanied him to the second-hand shop. Jones said he had come by the goods honestly.—Committed to the Quarter Sea- ssons for trial.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday morning a large congregation assem- bled at the Parish Church, Runcorn, to witness the celebration of the nuptials of Mr. George N. Grounds, eldest son of Mr. William Grounds, Dock Hotel, Weston Point, and Miss S. A. Thompson; the younger daughter of Mr. Arthur Thompson, the Mona, Higher Runcorn, and granddaughter of the late Mr. Samuel White, Run- corn. The wedding party began to arrive shortly before half-past eleven, and soon after that time the bride entered the sacred edifice. She looked very pretty being attired in a dress of rich ivory duchesse satin, trimmed with pearls and duchesse lace. She also wore sprays -f orange blossom and myrtle, as well as a long tulle veil and wreath. Her jewellery consisted of gold bracelets, the gift of the bridegroom. She was accompanied by four bridesmaids, namely, Miss Edith Thompson (sister of the bride), Miss Lily Grounds (sis- ter of the bridegroom), Miss A. Owen (Runcorn), and Miss A. Lowe (Bartington). They wore costumes of white corduroy cloth, with sleeves and sashes of ywllow bengaline, as well as large white drawn hats trimmed with yellow chrysanthemums. They carried bouquets to match, and wore gold brooches arid brace- lets, the gifts of the bride and bridegroom. Mr. T. J• Grounds occupied the position of best man. The officiat- ing clergyman was the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn. The party repaired to the residence of the bride, where between 40 and 50 guests, Sat down to breakfast. Several toasts followed. Shortly after two o'clock the happy pair left for Scot- land. The bride's travelling dress WAS of pale amethyst coloured cloth, trimmed with a darker shade of velvet, with vest of gold brocade; velvet hat with feathers to match. The presents were numerous and costly.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

It has been officially announced that Mr. Timmis, who has served as chairman of this important body for mny years past, has definitely decided to retire from the Board. This announcement, which was not, how- ever, unexpected, will doubtless be received with regret by all sections of the community. The Church party, as soon as it was definitely known that Mr. Timmls would not allow himself to be nominated, took steps to secure another candidate. They have been successful in this, the Rev. G. H. Garret, 8.D., vicar of Widnes, having c.nsented to seek election. The other retiring Church representatives, viz., Major Waring, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and Mr. C. E. Barlow, will be re-nomin- ated. The Nonconformist parts- have chosen Mr. B. Brown, the retiring member, and Messrs. H. Shaw and D. Lewis to contest the election on their behalf. A rumour was set afloat at one time that the Catholic party intended to run six candidates. The resolve, it ever made, however, has been abandoned. It is now under- stood that Mr. C. Flynn, gronel , tann-st., will he selected to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Dr. McDonnell, and the retiring members, viz., the Rev. Dean Fir.egan, the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Kee:Te, and Mr. S. Quinn, will be re-nominated.

div.head: EXTENSIVE JEWEL ROBBERY.
div.p: THE EXTENSIVE JEWEL ROBBERY.

At Lambeth, on Tuesday, William Kemp,Frederick Miles, and William Charles Neal were charged, the former with complicity in a jewel robbery, and the others with unla wild possession. Dm ing July a horss and pliap.on containitm jewellery, to the value of £4,200 were ,tolen from Lambeth, and the prisoners were arrested with a portion of the proceeds of the robbery in their posses- sion. Among such proceeds were loose diamonds, gold watches, and a gold and pearl pin.—The prisoners were remanded.
A meeting of cotton operatives at Rochdale on Thurs- day night unanimously resolved to resist the reduction of 5 per cent, in wages proposed by the Employers' Federation.

11,17 SCORN RURAL SANITARY • AU MO RIT I. THE BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Board-room, Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present J. Mclntyre (chairman), the Key. J. W. N. tanner, Messrs J Knowles, H. E. Heywood, E. Aaron, P. Hall, J. Whitlow. E. Bretherton, W. Whitlow, W. Turner, J. M. Williams, and J. Brnndreth ; Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.) CnOLERA pitECSIITIONS. The Clerk read the correspondence with reference to this matter with the Runcorn Commissioners, as to pro- viding accommodation, should a case of cholera come into the district. The following committee was appointed to deal with cases of emergency should any arise :—Messrs. Aaron, Stokes, Heywood, Williams, and Brandreth. DRLINAOR T RELSBY. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, enclosing a copy from Mr. F. B. Mason, solicitor. Chester, referritig to the above matter, which stated that the action of the Sanitary Authority in letting matters slide was most reprehensible. The Local Government Board's communication intimated that they proposed to ask one of their inspectors, when lie was next in the locality to confer with the Authority on the matter, the time and date to be forwarded. It was considered that the Authority would be ready to deal with the matter on the Inspector's visit. THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE AT RUNCORN. Mr. Heywood read the report of the committee appointed to consider this question. It stated that they had met the Runcorn Board of Commissioners on Sep- tember 14th, when it was pointed out that the bridge would cost about £140,000, but that there were rights and privileges, which would be interfered with, for which compensation would have to be paid, which, with other expenses, would probably amount to. about £BO,OOO, making a total cost of about £200,000. It was shown that the revenue derived from the ferry and foot- way across the river was about £5,000 per annum. after a lengthy discussion the committee were requested to consider in what way the authority could help forward the movement. The committee, after fully considering the matter, reported that if such a bridge were constructed it was expected that the Authority would contribute to the expense, and would c:iarge their rates with a fair proportian thereof. But a.suming that tolls would be levied for passing over the bridge, and that the revenue derived from the ferry and f.ootwav was about £5,000 per annntn, ann that the re- venue for a vehicular bridge would and considerably to that amount, the charge upon their rates would be com- paratively nil. (2). That such a bridge was very de- sirable, and independently of Runcorn, would be of great advantage to the agricultural portions of their Authority's district, inasmuch as it would open out new markets to them for agricultural produce, and would ultimately tend to lessen the railway rates between their district and other largo towns on the Lancashire side. (3). That such a bridge would directly greatly enhance the rateable value of property in Runcorn, and the town- ships in the Authority's district near thereto, and in- directly would benefit the whole of the locality, inasmuch as the rateable value of Runcorn and the townships near being thereby increased, the rates of the remaining townships would be thereby diminished. (4.) That the committee had not been able at present to verify the statements of the Com- missioners' committee, but consider it is well worthy the Authority's consideration, how far they would go in charging their rates for the erection of the bridge. (5.) That considering the advantages of such a bridge, the committee should be associated with their Clerk in attending with the committee of the Runcorn Imrrove- tnent Commissioners the next meetings of the County Councils of Cheshire and Lancashire. Continuing, Mr. Heywood said the report simply boond them to watch matters. If the County Councils would erect the bridge. the Authority would have no objection, but, if it was a case of that Union levying an amount on the rates, then they would have to go into the subject mere closely. There was little doubt that the scheme would prove highly advantageous, for they would be able to travel by , vehicles without going round by Warrington. It was expected that the greatest opposition would come from the railway company, for the provision of the bridge would undoubtedly reduce their rates. Thus the people would be benented.—Mr. Aaron • considered that the inhabitants of the district gener- ally would receive benefit the bridge were erected. . The cost of carriage of agricultural produce to many towns in Lancashire would be lessened.— Mr. W. Whitlow thought the bridge would be self-sup- porting.—On the motion of Mr. Williams, seconded by : Mr. Hall, the report was adopted, and authority was given to the committee to attend the County Council meetings.

div.head: TYPHOID FEVER AT WESTON.
div.p: TYPHOID FEVER AT WESTON.

Dr. Adams,-ir;Ti.; report, stated that two cases of typhoid fever had occurred at Weston Point, the causes being defective sanitation. Two similar cases had mani- fested themselves at Weston. He had examined a filthy, overcrowded,and dilapidated cottage at Walton Inferior, and he certified that the cottage,in its present condition, was unfit for habitation.
NUISANCE AT LOWER STRETTON.

A communication was r;S-d- from Mr. Robert Davies,of Warrington, in referench to a nuisance at Lower Beret- ton.—The Inspector stated that in order to abate the nuisance in a permanent manner the main sewer should be improved and extended, and he was diredted to ob- tain tenders for such to be done, and submit the same to ttt next meeting. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Board, held on Tnesday afternoon, at the Dutton Workhouse, there were present—Mr. J. Mclntyre (chairman), the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Lea, A. R. Norman, E. Aaron, A. Green- way, Joseph Knowles, John Whitlow, E. Jackson, T. Baxter, C.C., H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, T. Lewis, James Brandreth, P. Hall, William Ellison, E. Bretherton, J. Hall, W. Whitlow, J. Wilkinson, and W. Turner; Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. G. Ashton (deputy-clerk).
THE DIETARY TABLES.

The Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board, dated September 17th, asking for a I reply to their letter of January 19th, with reference to the dietary and ingredient tables at the workhouse. fie explained what had beer done, and that their present system was the one recommended by the medical officer of health, and the committee had decided that it should not be altered. Mr. Brandreth stated that the commit- ter considered that the inmates of their Union got better fed than those in the workhouses of other unions. They gave them more potatoes, bacon, milk, &c., in which there was more nutriment than in the food supplied elsewhere.

div.head: CONTRACTS.
div.p: THE CONTRACTS.

The tenders for contracts for provisions and supplies for the year ending March 25th, 1893 were opened, and those of the following tradesmen were accepted :—Mr. Richardson, coal ; Mr. Sharrack, shoes ; Mr. Lightfoot, coffins; the Sanitas Company, soap and disinfectants ; Messrs. Unsworth, Brothers, clothing ; Mr. Thomas Wright, drapery ; Mr. Whitlow, straw ; Mr. Grounds for carting ; Mr. Jackson, for removing paupers and gen- eral cartage from Runcorn, and far removing lunatics to asylums ; Mr. Collier. grocezies ; Mr. Gill, butchers' meat ; and Mr. I. Speakman, drugs. This was all the business of importance.

div.head: RUNCORN CASE OF CHILD STEALING.
div.p: THE RUNCORN CASE OF CHILD STEALING.

A somewhat remarkable case of child stealing came before the magistrates at the Romford Police Court on Thursday. A girl of 17, named Elizabeth Chapman, alias Carke, was charged with stealing- a boy named Twitchett, aged two years, from Rom ford in May last. The prisoner was traced to Runcorn, and it was discovered she had plac-d the child under the care of a schoolmistress. She stated that she loved the boy ; and she had evi- dently been very kind and attentive to him, and he manifested undoubted affection for her. Prisoner was committed for trial at the Essex Quarter Sessions.

div.head: SUPPOSED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH
div.p: SUPPOSED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH
AT FARNWORTIL

Yesterday morning,at Widnes Police Court.before Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, a slight, delicate-looking girl named Annie Firth,aged 18,who lives at The Horns, Farnworth, with her parents, was charged upon her own confession with having, on the 16th August, concealed the birth ofiter child. Mr Knowles appeared ' on her behalf.--Superintendent Keighley informed his Worship that the girl gave herself up to the police that morning, saying that she li comealed the birth of her child. She could not eay whether it was a male or female child, but she said it was horn about five o'clock on the morning ot the 16;11 of last month. kept the child in the bed until the Afternoon, when her mother left the house to go to Widnes. She then wrapped the child in a piece of brown paper and put it in the ashpit. The body had not been found yet, but he had sent a sergeant and i a constable to look for t. A post-mortem and inquest have to he beret..., he 3Skt• i for prisoner to be remanded to the cells until Monday. The prisoner was accordingly remanded to the cells until Monday.

Herr Edward Strauss, the famous composer, is lying so dangerously ill at Vienna that only slight hopes are entertained of his recovery. The Duke of Devonshire has intimated to the Bishop of Southwell his decision to exercise the right of presen- ltation to certain benefices in Derbyshire, which right the late duke had latterly entrusted to the bishop.

BEFORE TEUE MA.GISTRATES.

NOTTINGHAM Yours TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET. Two lads named Harry Wright and Joseph Ball were charged before the Warrington borough magistrates on Wednesday with riding by rail on Tuesday from Stock- port to Warrington without a ticket. They had walked from Nottingham, they said, being out of employment and not liking to be dependent on their parents; and they had ridden from Stockport in a third class of a Midland train. Evidence was given that they tried to pass themselves off as brothers and pretended that their father had their tickets. They were ordered to pay the fare Is. 6d. or go to jail for seven days. THEFT OF A CONCERTINA Box. At the borough police court on Monday, Wm. llig- ginson, labourer, 32, Stamford-street, was charged with stealing, en Saturday night, at the Greyhound beerhouse Dalton-lane, a concertina box, the property of Hermann Dean, forge labourer. It appeared that the prosecutor was playing the concertina in the house, and put it in the box under the seat, and found afterwards that the box was gone, though net the instrument. The landlord closed the doers, and desired to know who had left the house when it was ascertained that the prisoner had. P.C. Cooper and Ser- geant Cheeney and two other constables went to his house late at night, and surrounded the house, but could get no answer at the door. One of the con- stables got over the wall, and the house was found in darkness and the prisoner on the sofa with a box near him. In reply to the constable he said he had no answer to make to the charge.—The defendant now admitted taking the box, but said he had had a drop of drink and did not know what he was doing.—Mr. Shaw, landlord of the Greyhound, made an unsworn statement that the defendant was perfectly sober in his house.—The Chair- man said his defence was clearly untrue.—lnspector Jones said the man pretended to be drunk when appre- hended. He was fined 20s. and costs, or 14 days. A RAID TJPON STREET OBSTIICCTORS. At the borough pslice court on Monday, the following cases were heard :—Edward Connor, Sankey-st., was charged with allowing a cab to stand an hour and forty minutes to the obstruction of passengers, in King-st., on the 14th inst. 'I he cab had no horse harnessed to it. 10s. and costs. tVin. White, farmer, Fearnhead, for allowing a horse and cart to stand in Market-st., on Saturday morning, was fined 103. including costs. John Mcginn was charged with allowing a bus to stand in San- key-st ~ on the 15th inst.—The 'bus had no horse attached to it,which the Chairman remarked made the offence wore —Ho was fined 10:s including costs.—William greengrocer, Gclden Grove-st., for allowing a hand cart to stand an unwarrantable time in Horsemarket-street, was fined ss. including costs.—John Hibbert,contractor, Moss Side, Manchester, charged with allowing a quantity of bricks and rubbish to stand, on the morn- ing of the 1091 inst., in Bridge-st., was fined Si. includ- ing costs. THEFT OF £lB BY A YOUNG WOMAN. At the Warrington magistrates' court on Wednesday, before Councillor James Fairclough (chairman), and Aldermen Wright and Francomb, Elizabeth Rutherford, domestic servant, aged 21, was charged with stealing on Tuesday £lB the property of her brother, Thos. Ruther- ford, Ship Canal labourer, with whom she lived at 4 Gray-st., off Hopwood-st., School Brow.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been in service at Grap- penhall, but came home in consequence of her mother being seriously ill. OH Sunday, about noon, Thomas Rutherford, her brother put in a purse in a box, which he locked, the sum of £lB. The prisoner's mother during Tuesday heard something which caused her to tell her husband and son when they came home at night to go and look at 'Thomas's box. They did so, and found that the £lB had gone. About eight o'clock that night they were walking down Buttermarket-st. when they met the prisoner with a young woman and two soldiers, all under the influence of drink, and she began to scream and make a noise to draw a crowd. She was given into the custody of Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, who brought her to the police station. She there gave up £ll 123. 31d. and also a watch, chain, and two rings. She said silo had been short of pocket money, and had put the things in pledge and redeemed them, so that nearly £l4 of the stolen money was accounted for. The remainder had gone in eating and drinking,not so much for what she had had herself as for what others_had had which she had paid for.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.— George Rutherford and D.S. Monaghan made a corro- borative statement, and said the prisoner told him she took £2 on Monday and £l6 on Tuesday. He had not had much trouble with her, and she had never taken anything out of the house before. He afterwards said they could do nothing with her at home.—She was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. MINOR CASES.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATIIRDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (chairman): and _ . _ ... ..
Mr. J. Geddes.
DRUNK.--John Smith, from Leicestershire, drunk in Battersby-lane early that morning, was fined ss. and costs.

WANTED FOR WIFE DESERTION.—SamueI Wilkinson was brought up,lie being wanted by the Hartlepool police on a charge of deserting his wife arid six children there. He was ordered to be detained till the arrival of a Hartle- pool constable.
SiONDLY.—tefore Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and Sutton.

ASSAULTING His FATHEEL.—Thos. Edward Griffiths, aged 25, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting his father, with whom he lived at 32, Tanners'-lane. P.S. Taylor said he heard a disturbance in the house, and on going there found the defendant holding a spade in a threatening attitude and using threateßing language to him.—The prosecutor gave cor- roborative evidence, and the defendant was bound over in his own recognisances for £5 and a surety of £5 to keep the peace six months. DEUWIC AND DISORDERLY.—John Baguley, a hawker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Market Place, and assaulting P.C. Clarke there, on Saturday night. Clarke said he was drunk and creat- ing a disturbance because he was not allowed to serve at a stall. On his taking him into custody he tripped him up and kicked him, and in struggling he knocked over a pair of scales, value a sovereign, and broke them.— Corroborative evidence was given, and Mrs. Lightfoot's daughter proved the destruction of the scales, One month's imprisonment.—Wm. Boyle, fustian cutter, from Crewe, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly, on Saturday night, in Winwick-road, also with hawking boot laces without a license ; and fined ss. and costs.—Catherine Ryan, married woman, drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st.,on Sunday morning, 53. and costs.—James Bowcock, at Bridge Foot, on Sat- urday night, who had refused to pay his bus fare, but had paid it, fined ss. including costs.—David Gough was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Market- St., the same night. A constable said he was drunk and very noisy, and he told him that a trap had run over his foot. Ile examined the foot, and found it had just been grazed. He refused to walk, but one of his friends came up and said, "If thou doesn't walk, I'll smash thy yead off," and then he could walk quite well. (Laugh- ter.) ss. including costs.—Mary Hayes, in Buckley-st., on the same night, 2s. 6J.—Patrick Kilroy, in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, 53. and costs.
• • D11172;134 AND REFUSING TO QUIT.—John Sullivan, Ship Canal labourer, charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Royal arms, Sank-street, was fined ss. and •nsts.

FICIITING.—James Fletcher, shoemaker, 35 Greenall- st., and David Walsh, 49 Bewsey-st., who did not appear, were charged with fighting on the night of the 11th inst., in florsemarket-st.—Mr. Browne defended, and said Walsh had gone to Scotland temporarily. He did not know whether Walsh knew of the summons or not. Fletcher was hound over to keep the peace for six months, and bad to pay costs. AN lixt.iceNstm Do.—George Pugh, 55 Catherine-st., was charged with keeping a dog without a license, and fiord 5;. and costs. _
PITCII AND Toss—John Griffin. a boy, described as a vagrant, 13th appearance, was fined Sc. and costs for playing at pitch and toss for money on Sunday after- noon. _ _

Tuaowimo Coat..—George Fearnley, 12, 38 Hardy-st., 3rd appearance, and Michael Burke, 10, 34 (lee-st., were chard with throwin4 pieces of coal in the last-named street on Saturday. Fearnley was fined 25., and Burke

TUESDAY.—Bgore Mr. Garnett and Major Nicholson. A DESERTEEL—AIfred Drew, charged with being a deserter from the Royal Fusiliers, was remanded to Strangeways Gaol to await the arrival cf the military escort.

FINED FOR BEING DRUNlC.—Michael Hofferty, Joseph Hart.—Annie Ryan was sent to prison for fourteen days, for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street on the previous evening. WEDNESDAY.—BeforeCouncillor James Fairclough (chair- man), and Aldermen Wright and Francomb. ASSAULTING His WlFE.—George T. Patrick was charged with assaulting his wife in Green-street, on Wednesday night. A constable deposed to witnessing the assault, and his sons tryine to separate the c:efendant frem her.—The wife also gave evidence, and said her husband used horrible language to her, the defendant remarking: Best have a separation old girl.—His wife, in reply to the Bench, said she would ask for aseparation, and accept 104. a week.—The defendant said his wife had called him a rotten devil, and the lad had picked up the poker to strike him, ,and all four got on to him.— He was cotnmttted to prison for 14 days, his wife being granted a separation order, with 103. a week. CHARGE OF STEALING A HEN.—Thomas Creear was brought up on remand from the Occasional Court, charged with stealing a hen, value 2s. 6d., from the barn of Thomas Hampson, farmer, Rixton. Mr. Browne defended.—Mr. Hampson gave evidence, expressing the opinion that the affair was a drunken spree on the part of the prisoner.—Sergeant Barnes deposed to finding the defendant lying in the barn about one o'clock the pre- vious morning, with the hen quite warm, and recently killed, at his feet. Witness asked him what he was doing there,and he replied" nothing." He charged hi.n with stealing the hen, and he made no reply.—ln answer , to Mr. Browne witness said the hen, produced, was flat as though the defendant might have fallen on it. He was not drunk.—Mr. Browne said his client was drunk, and as he lived with a farmer closely adjoining, had got into the barn by mistake and fallen upon the hen and crushed it. He read a letter from the Rev. Father Myerscough giving the defendant an excellent character, and expressing the belief that the matter was the result of a drunken spree.—The prisoner's employer was called and spoke highly of his character, and said lie believed the matter was a drunken tnistake.—The de- fendant was ordered to pay costs. THURSDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley (chairman), and Sutton and Mr. John Fairclough. A MILITARY ABSENTEE.—Francis Ryan was charged with being an absentee from the training of the 3rd Liverpool militia. He pleaded that he had been away at sea, He was fined 40s. ;in default,l4 days imprison- ment with hard labour. TITEFT or A SHlRT.—Patrick Connelly,farm labourer, was charged with stealing, on Monday, a shirt the pro- perty of Luke Cadeney, rag gatherer. They had lodged together at 18 Percival's Fold, and the prisoner had stolen the shirt from the lodgings. He was sent to prison for 14 Itys with hard labour. ON ENCLOSED PREMISES.—Wm. John Heaston was charged with being found on the premises of Messrs. Kenyon and Co., Bank Quay, at half-past 11 the previous night, with intent to commit a felony.—A Constable said in consequence of a report that a watch had been stolen at Messrs. Kenyon's about ten o'clock, and that the prisoner and other strange men had been seen about the place, witness went to the works and found the prisoner there, but, on searching him, found no watch. —Other evidence having been given,the prisdlner pleaded that he was on the works to stop all night there.—The prisoner, who had been up nine or ten times previously for like offences, was sent to jail for a month. NON-PAYMENT OF RATES.—Orders were made against several persons for non-payment of rates ; and several others were excused, on their application, from payment. BREACHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT.—The following per- sons were dealt with on the prosecution of Mr. G. Riley, School Attendance Officer, for the above-named offences :—Elizabeth Deakin, hawker, 23, Beswick-st. ; John Heaton, paviour, 31, Back Howard-st. ; Peter Garland, forgeman, 73, Watkin-st. ; Thomas Moody, forgeman, 38, Pierpoint-st. ; William Farrington, I labourer, Pierpoint-at. ; Martin Carey, forgeman, Bake- house Yard ; John Craddock, signalman, 192, Longford- st. ; William France, 24, Watkin-st. ; Edwin Stacey, forgeman, 18, Refuge Square ; and Michael Kenna, Ship Canal man, 52, Lord Nelson-st. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and Wright and Dr. Gornall. UNSEEMLY CONDUCT.—EIiza Henderson for unseemly , conduct in Bewsev-st., was discharged. CRUELTY TO A HORSE—James Clare, 83, Church-st., for working a horse while in an unfit state, was fined 10s. and costs.
THREATENING.—EIiza Brady. 14, Bucklev-st., was charged with threatening Ellen Hannaghan, 12,Buek ley- st., but dismissed.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. J.. J. Bleckley.

SLEEPING ON A CORN STACIL—Three men, named Thos. Browne, Joseph Hagan, and J. Peak, were charged with sleeping on a corn stack at Haydock,on Monday evening, without permission. Sergeant Sage proved the case. He said that towards early morning,whilst on duty near Blackbrook, he found the three prisoners on the stack. He discovered their presence through the men creating a noise.—The prisoners stated that they were on their way to Sc. Helens from Liverpool, and the reason that they were induced to adopt thestack as a night's lodging was because it was very wet, late, and dark, and they could not procure any lodgings in the houses of the district.— The case was dismissed.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

WEDNmsn's..y—.2-ii-e-fore Mr. John Crosfield (chairman),and Mr S. R. Armitage. DRUNK.--Margaret Ruskin, drunk at Croft on the night of the 22nd ult., 2s. 6d. and costs.—John Perrin, drunk at Riaton, on the 10th inst., 53. and costs.— Robert Whitfield, at Poulton, on the 17th inst., 103., and costs. CHARGE OF DAMAGING TURNIPS.—Frank Hall and George Knott, boys, were charged with doing damage, on the let inst., to turnips, the property of George Cook farmer, Orford. Mr. Jenkins defended.—A constable having given evidence against the defendants, the prose- cutor did the like, and said he had had 30 cwt. of tur- nips destroyed by lads.—Mr. Jenkins said the defendants went into the field to look for a ball, and though they did not find it, it was found subsequently by Mr.Camm, proving the truth of Knott's previous statement.—The lads were called in each others' defence, and other bays. and Mr. Camm, were als) called.—The Bench dismissed the case. FIGHTING.—John Gandy, a young man, was charged with fighting with Henry Dando, at Penketh. on the 3rd inst.—Martin Churchill and Charles Grahame,with fight- ing., at Collins Green, on the Gth inst. All four defen- dants were bound over to keep the peace, and had to pay costs. CYCLING ON THE I.OO'MA-in.—Ernest Carter, of War- rington, for riding a bicycle on the footpath at Great Sankey, on Sunday morning, was fined 23. 6d. and costs.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit and C. Reynolds. LODGING-HOUSE KEEPER FlNHD.—Thomas Frane, Mersey-street, Runcorn, lodging-house keeper, was sum- moned, for refusing to give access to a part of his premises, to P.S. Gosling, when required on the 11th inst. Mr. Burton represented defendant.—P.S. Gosling stated that on Sunday night, at 10.45, he went to defendant's lodging-house, and saw a nutnberof people. He asked how many lodgers he had, and received the reply eight, the number for which he was registered. He noticed considerably more, and therefore asked him who was upstairs. He received the reply " a boy." Defendant refused to admit witness into one of the rooms, saying it was a private one. He demanded admission, but Frane said one should enter.—Mr. Burton contended that the sergeant went. upstairs, looked into the rooms, and when about to enter the one in question, his client made objection, saying it was his own private bedroom, and no other officer had ever desired to go in. —Finedl2s. 6d. and costs. or 14 days. THE SALE OF MARGAIIINE.—James Byrne, 35, Church- st., Runcorn, provision dealer, was summoned for ex- posing for sale margarine, without having it marked or labelled, as required by the Margarine Act, 1887, on August 20th. A similar charge was preferred against John Morris, of Bridge-st., Runcorn. committed on the same date. Inspector Hallard spoke to visiting the shop of Mr. Byrne on the date named, and to asking for some butter ticketed 10d. When serving him the man in the shop said it was margarine.—Defendant Byrne said he had no intention to defraud. He had not the word "margarine" on the article, but it was always wrapped in specially marked papers. The Bench considered the case proved, and imposed a fine of 10s. and Bs. 6d. costs. —The case against Morris was of a similar nature, the word, however, facing the wrong way, and not in view of the customer, as required by the Act.—Fined 10s. and 93. 6d. costs.

A SUSPECTED PICIPocKET.—Thomas Kelly, alias Peter Kelly, hailing from Warrington, was charged with fre- quenting the Market-place, Runcorn,with intent to com- mit a felony, at nine p.m. on Saturclay. --P.C. Jewitt spoke to receiving information at the police station that prisoner was in the Market-place, and that he had been trying to pick a woman's pocket. He went there, and watched him for an hour. Prisoner tried to get among groups of women, and several times Stooped down, but 0 as not seen to take anything. One wo'man reported

the loss of her purse, and Kelly no doubt had confeder- ates in the crowd.—Prisoner, who said he had no inten- tion to commit a felony, was sent to gaol for 14 days. DRUNICHNNESS.—EIizabeth Cox, Fountain-brow, Run- corn ; James Millington, Henry Lowe, John Prager, and Michael O'Brien.—A. warrant was issued against Patrick Corcoran, Mersey-st., Runcorn, for drunkenness, he fail- ing to answer his summons.

WIDNES POLICE COURT.' MONDAY.—Before Messrs. EL Wade Deacon and F. A. Stapleton Bretherton. DRUNKENNESS. —James Dempsey, Milwood-street ; Dominic Dovitch, Water-street ; Richard Elowcroft, no fixed abode ; and Charles Nolan, no fixed abode, were charged with being drunk and disorderly, and fined 2s. 61 and costs each, or seven days in default.

SLIMING °QT.—Patrick Burns, no fixed abode, was charged with sleeping in a shed in Lugsdale-road, about half-past three on Sunday morning, without having any visible means of subsistence. P.C.'s Messenger and Dur- ham proved the case.—On promising not to repeat the offence, defendant was discharged. .

A WARNING TO Bors.—Al-exander li.eglian (14), Beaumont-street, and William Fra3er (14), Terrace-road, were charged with stealing a piece of timber, valued at 2d. A man named Parry said he WAS the owner of a dis- used flat, lying on the shore at Westbank, and damage to the extent of £4O had been dme to it by lads breakiag pieces off it.—Both lads pleaded guilty, and were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1892,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1892,
FOOTBALL.

. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bowsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RNNGERS.-THE FinsT LEADERS OF THE LEAGUE.

The ineffable honour, says " Philistine " in the " Athletic News," the mighty distinction of being the first to figure at the head of the Lancashire League table belongs to Warrington. How long they will stay there is another story altogether, but there they are, and for the present they can lay the flattering unction to their soles that they have achieved that which no other Lan- cashire club has ever done and can ever do. True, it is not a very important matter, neither is the glory of a lasting description, for that sublime state of ecstacy ha which they now revel may be changed in a few brief weeks to a more sober and less enthusiastic kind of existence, but while the name of the Warrington Club proudly fills the highest place, let us do the players honour. It was not by a mere whiff of Victory's breath that they soared to the dizzy height, but by the cyclonic movement of the brawny arms of Triumph. (You may take the above sentence and wipe your feet upon it, yet it will not shrink, neither will the colour fade.) How mud' of this remarkable performance of the Warrington men is duo to the fact that in their ranks the only Plumpton is now enrolled the modern and modest re- corder of things oannot say ; he can only mention the fact and leave the discerning public to think their own thinks. It is too colossal an item to treat flippantly or without grave consideration, and therefore I will leave the subject for the present, and return to it when the Ship Canal Ordinary shareholders are drawing big dividends.

There are many things about • the Warrington Club to admire, and though one could not help being struck on Saturday with the delightful view of the splendid field, the beautiful surroundings, and the completeness of the arrangements, the one groat fact that punctuality is also numbered among the tnany attributes of the Warrington Club will ever endear it to my memory. A few minutes before the appointed time the teams came on the field, and at the proper moment the game was started. This departure from the usual procedure of other clubs is a novelty and deserves recording. Of course, the visitors are quite as much entitled to any praise that may be flying about as the home team, and if I had been giving prizes away this week, they would certainiy have got a few. However, in order that I may remember them in future, I just pop their names in here. Warrington.—J. Boscow, back ; F. Plumpton, F. Heesorn. and C. Potts, three-quarter backs; Jno. Bate, and J. W. Evans, half-backs • H. Ashton, Fair Turner, , Frank Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, W. Raudles, J. Holmes, W. Berry, and T. Donoghue, forwards. Broughton Rangers.—J. Hacking, back; E. Gresty and J. W. Parks, and J. allcock, three-quarter backs; T. Wall and W. Hughes, half backs ; J. Jackson, R. Medley, S. Oman, J. Thomas, J. Nowell, J. Fitton, J. Cleminson, J. Shaw, and S. Hall, forwards. Referee : Mr. R. Wilcock (Liverpool). It was clearly evident five minutes after Frank Turner had kicked off that the Rangers were not a match for their more weighty and combined opponents. The home team attacked at once, and the visitors were actively engaged in repulsing the enslaueht. Passing by Bate, Evans, and Heesom carried hostilities nigh to , the Rangers' goal, and there a rush by the forwards,and ' a smart bit of work by Plumpton, ended in Berry scam- pering over the line and securing a try. Frank Turner did not improve the point. That try was the only tan- ' gible result of the first half, though play was continually in the Rangers' quarters. The smart and clever passing and running by the Warrington backs, and the fine,' vigorous style of the forwards, was mainly responsible for the repeated attacks on the visitors' goal. Plumpton tried to drop a goal, but it was only a left-footed effort, while Potts was just frustrated on the line,after a dash- ing sprint, and Donoghue failed when a try seemed a certainty. The defensive powers of the Rangers were put to a severe test, hut the splendid play of Hacking, Gresty, Allcock, and Hughes, with the sturdy help of the forwards, of whom Jackson, M`Gowan, and Oman were the most conspicuous, prevented any further scoring. It was when the second half was fairly under weigh that the Warrington combination emerged from its retire- ment, as it were, and became more actively militant. A touchdown was the first indication of the pressure,and then Nevin electrified the crowd by his smartness, and the subsequent movements ended in a good bit of pas- sing by Evans, Bate, and Potts, by which the last- named was enabled to scoot over the line at the corner. The difficult place was taken by Plumpton, arid a clever shot failed by a few inches. A fese minutes afterwards, relics, who is not a whale on pas- sing, managed to make up his mind to part with the ball, and did so in such a ridiculous man- ner, that Plumpton intercepted, and the latest naturalised burgess of :the town shot away in his own inimitable style, and scored a grand try from which Heesom kicked a goal. After restarting from centre, the Rangers played with better combination, and after Medley's individual effort, Gresty's noble exertions, and Joe Shaw's dexterous dribble, the warfare was of an oven nature. Both sides were very smart., though the home team always held the upper hand. Evans missed a nice chance to drop at goal, preferring to pass across to Fleesom. who in turn flung the leather rather wildly to Plumpton, with the inevitable consequence that the , opportunity slid away at the same time. Jolley livened things up somewhat when he started a dribble that transferred the scene of play near the Rangers' line, and though Hacking got rid of the danger very warily, Jolley dashed away again, and this time he got the leather over the line for Fleesoin to score a try and Plumpton to fail at goal. Parks distinguished himself after this by appearing to labour under the remarkable hallucination that he was playing the whole of the Warrington men himself. Alter he had been knocked down several times he gave the matter up as a bad job. Potts made a grand run, but was held on the line by M'Gowan and Hacking, and while this interesting struggle was going on Holmes ran behind the posts, and then, on the referee's order took the ball back where he had found it. .A slight struggle in the near proximity ended in Nevins giving the leather to Evans,who despite his gory head, got a try, which was not improved by the place kick of Plumpton. With this item the pro- ceedings were brought to a close, the score standing thus :—Warrington, 1 goal, 4 tries; Broughton Rangers, nothing. The Rangers were never really dangerous. They were outclassed 'by the Warrington men, and never made a combined effort during the whole of the game. There was nothing approaching an understanding visible in their movements, and to this fact more than anything else the decisive defeat may be put down. There are many men among the Rangers who possess the requisite talent that make good footballers, but there is something more than individual excellence wanted nowadays. The whole team must work like one man, the contingent must be actuated by one desire, and that to score. It does not matter a continental whether it is Tom this or Jack that who gets the try or kicks the goal, but it mekes all the difference to the Rangers whether the club is defeated or gains a triumph. On Saturday the play of some of the team showed a lamentable lack of unity of purpose. Hugging the ball until half a dozen men hug you is not exactly football ; it is more like a phase in a wrestling match. That kind of play was observed on , many occasions, and it always resulted in the discom- fiture of the Rangers. A centre three-quarter who ignores the existence of his wing men, in the same style that Parks did, does not deserve to have his photo talon with a Rangers' jersey on. The halves were smart and fairly tricky, but have yet something to learn to over- come such clever men as those of Warrington. The for- wards had plenty of vigour. but not much idea of unanimity. Gresty and A:cock did well when they had anything to do. On the Warrington side the same old smartness behind was seen. The fine passing game which the back division play, if not quite as finished in style as I have seen before, was still animating the players. Plumpton can play a good game when he likes, and when he is not self-conscious, On Saturday

he showed his ability, and there is a possibility that he may yet be seen in more important fixtures. Evans is still the same sturdy, skilful player, and both Heesotn and Potts made a favourable impression. Among the forwards Ashton, Turner, Jolley, Handles, and Nevins were very prominent, but the whole body of the for- wards were as formidable as ever. WARRINGTON A V. BROUGHTON RANGERS A.—Both sides were strongly represented for the above match, which was played on the new ground of the Rangers. The game was not of an exhilarating character at the com- mencement. line-outs and scrimmaging following with a regularity that grew monotonous, until J. Lawless by a smart piece of work neutralised a dribble of the home team. A vigorous rush by Davies, Thornley. Newoy. and Teare transferred the scene of operations further into the home lines, but the pressure was relieved and the leather forced to Ashurst, who replied with a fine kick, and a minor was conceded. Then Deakin was conspicuous on behalf of the Broughtonians, but Bailey and Westall dribbled away, Robinson being Moored at the quarter diag. Then for sometime the contest waged between the home 25 and half way, the football being, of the most wretched elescriptien at this part of the game, which was relieved by Newsy., Higham, Molyneaux,and Glover rushing, to their opponents' half, where a pretty bout of passing between Westall, Lally, and the brothers Lawless forced a miner. Woods and Ashurst for their respective sides were prominent, the latter time after time clearing his lines in splendid style. Another strong rush of the Warringtonians tested the opposing defence, and then a grand display of passing amongst the for- wards ended in J. Lawless running over. Barnes re- turned:the drop-out,but the over-zeal displayed by the visi- tors lost the advantage. Then the Rangers had a grand chanee of scoring., Woods running', right to the line, a for- ward pass spoiling the opportunity. Strong play cleared the danger, and a dribble headed by Warburtcn, Davies, Thornley, and Teare removed operations past midfield, a spell of passing between Warburton, Lally, and J. Law- less taking the oval under the posts, and half time arrived with Warrington 0-1-2 to nil. The brief rest had evidently an inspiring influence on the home team, for they at once got right on the Warrington line. A determined rush by the " wirepullers " soon drove the attackers back, and then ensued a magnificent piece of play. Barnes, who was now playing half back, smartly got the leather away to Lally, and after it had been transferred between J. and P. Lawless, the latter ran clean into his opponents' 25,and re-passed to his brother, who handed over to Thornley„ and a try was scored under the posts, Ashurst converting. The kick-off was charged, Fligliam, Thornlev, and Team again raising the siege, and another quick display of passing between Barnes, Lally, and J. Lawless resulted in a third try, whilst immediately after P. Lawless rushed over. Then Barnes made a grand run, but the Rangers retaliated, and amidst some loose play near midfield Harrison threw across to Deakin. who effected a fine run in. No sooner had the game been restarted than Lally, J. Law- less, and P. Lawless manipulated the ball splendidly, a strong run by the latter securing his second try. War- rington were playing magnificently, repeatedly revoking cheers from the crowd for their fine exhibition of pas- sing, and then Glover made a strong dribble. Again some fine passing between the halves and three quarters saw P. Lawless securing his third try, which Barnes converted. Directly afterwards Barnes scored, and placed a goal. Result—Warrington 4-3-3, Broughton Hangers 0-1-0. WARRINGTON( Sr. MARY'S V. FARNWORTEL—On Satur- day the above match was played at Warrington in very fine weather. The visitors won the tone, and played with a slight wind. The Saints started the ball, and at once took it inns the Farnworth 25. Bennett managed to get over, but the try was not allowed, and the Saints playing up the same player again got over. This time the point was allowed, no goal resulting. After the drop-out Farnworth rallied and were soon pressing, and after several scrimmages Femney dodged over and scored, but no goal was kicked. After the ball being again re-started, the defence on both sides was good, the backs of both teams kicking well, and the ball was kept about midfield, and up to half time the score was one try each. On turning round the Saints' forward played up hard, and had the ball on the Farnworth line. The visitors' backs kept returning time after time, but with- out avail, and Woods made a grand run and scored, the point not being improved. The hall being dropped out, the Sainte had all the game ; the visitors were thoroughly overplayed and could net keep their lines out of danger. After a bit cf good passing between Woods, Hampson, and Berry, the latter managed to get over, but the point was not allowed. After the drop out the Saints were again pressing, and soon Sanders ran over, the try again being disallowed, but the Saints were not to be done, as Helsby picked up and rushed over. but Sanders could not manage to improve the point when the whistle blew for time. Final score :—St. Mary's, 3 tries ; Farnworth, 1 try, 1 minor. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH v. CLAUGHTON (BIRKEN- , HEADI.—The Parish Church team played the first of their 'fixtures on Saturday, when they visited Claughton. , Rather a weak team gathered, and this was not im- proved by one of the players missing the train. A start was made with 14 men, and the home team playing down the slope were soon attacking. The visitors de- fended well, but Daniels met with an accident, and for the rest of the game the Parish practically had 13 players. Half-time arrived with no points scored, and on the re- start the home team took a turn at defending. Boles- worth, Hurst, Carey, and Welsby were in fine form, and the line was crossed twice by Ma.kio and Carey, both points, however, being disallowed. Just on the call of time a strong forward rush was made, and from a palp- able threw forward the home team scored. The point was appealed against, but the objection was overruled, and the result finally stood as follows :—Claughton, a try ; Parish Church, three minors. WARRINGTON PARISH CHUILCR V. ()LAUGHTON (2NO Tnams).—These teams opened the season on Saturday on the ground of tae former. The home captain won the toss, and the Parish played with the wind and sun in their favour during the first half. The visitors were soon pressed, and rarely did they break away past the half- way line. No points were scored during this portion, and the visitors' chances looked very rosy on the restart. The Parish, however, upset the calculations, and it was I not long before Atherten dropped a neat goal. Berry I Was next to score, and on the call of time, Duckworth broke away, and crossing to Archer when near the line, the second try was regis'ered, Appleton improving the ' point. Final score: Pariah Church 2nd, 2 goals, 1 try and 4 minors; Claughton 2nd, 2 minors. EARLESTOWN V. STOCKTON HriATEL—Earlestown opened their new ground on Saturday, before a good number of spectators, when they encountered a team from Stockton Heath. The game was very fast and exciting, Harrison, for Earlestown, making a splendid run from a pass by Croft, and succeeded in placiqg it between the uprights, finally improving his effort by securing a goal. He suc- ceeded in getting another in, but the distance being dis- puted, the place was not allowed. Stockton Heath made great efforts to equalise, but Earlestown ran out winners by 1 goal, 3 tries, to nil. WESTON POINT R.T.C. v. WARRINGTON ALBION.—The above match was played at Weston Point. on Saturday, before a good number of spectators. The game was very fast throughout, and nothing was scored in the first half but minors. Cookson scored a try for Weston Point a quarter of an hour before time, afterwards kicking a goal, and a very pleasant and even game ended.—Wes- ton Point, one goal two minors ; Warrington Albion, three minors. WARRINGTON 2NO V. ROCHDALE RANGERS—Payed at Warrington, the local team winning by three goals seven tries.

-- ASSOCIATION. WA RRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. HAYDOCK Sr. JAIL ES'S. These teams met on the Warrington new ground, Arpley, being the first time the clubs have met. War- rington kicked off, against a strong sun, about 3.45 p.m.' and were early on the aggressive, but the Haydock backs relieved, and the visitors' right wing raced towards Jones, Blacksmith scoring a beauty. The St. James's then kept up the pressure, soon after adding another goal. Warrington now livened up consider- ably, and made a strong attack. Eventually, from a throw in by Phillips, Dendy seored. • From the re-start the homesters were again round the Havdock citadel, Norman putting in a Lleauty adding number two. Half- time result.—Warrington two goals, flaydock two goals. Re-starting, the home forwards were at it again, but the visitors' custodian played grandly. Haydock, playing well up, from a bit of neat passing, added another point. From a free kick at the visitors'asnd, Warrington scored again, Norman equalising,. The Haydock team now played up, and again drew ahead, Jones misjudging a good shot. The home team, not to be outdone, played with renewed vigour, and again equalised from the foot of Forbes. Each side now strove to gain the winning point, but the whistle blew for time, the score being Warria.gton, four goals; Haydock St. James's, four goals. Warrington team: Goal, Jones •, full back, J. Kincaid, ' captain ; F. Davies, half backs ; J. Phillips, Mather, and F. Chidlaw ; forwards. F. Norman, R. Fennelly, T. P. Forbes, F. Denby, and S. Johnson. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION RESERVE V. FIAYDOCK Sr. JANES'S RESERVE.—The above match was played at Haydock in line weather, the visitors arriving with a weak team. Haydock kicked off with the sun against them, and after about 25 minutes' even play, the home team scored from a scrimmage in front of goat Half time arrived with the score—Haydock, one goal; War- rington nil. In the secoud half Warrington had hard lines; the forwards working the ball up the field, but could not score. After about ten minutes' play, Hay- doek scored. Soon after Swarbrick, one of the Warrington half-backs, retired, and Warrington finished the game with ten men, nothing further being scored Final result :—Slaydock, two goals ; Warrington, nil.
