WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board of Guar- dians was held on Wednesday. Owing to the existence of smallpox in the Workhouse, the meet- ing was held in tlie Council Chamber at the Town Hall, which had been placed at the service of the Guardians by the Mayor and Corporation. Mr. R. Heaton presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. P. Roberts, Messrs. Balharry, Davies, A. J. Jolley, W. Houghton, Clarke, Mather, Turton,Smith, Dobson, P.iirclough, Kilsham, Longton, A. Jolley, Muir, Dignun3, Hill, Gill, Hood-Wright, Pilling, Shaw, Aukland ; S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and other officials.

div.head: THANKING TUE CORPORATION.
div.p: THANKING TUE CORPORATION.

Mr. Davies moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor and Tewn Council for allowing them the use of that splendid room for the transaction of their business that morning, and for a short time i the future. He thought that if any occasion arose in the future whereby they could reciprocate the kind feeling displaced 6v the Corpora- tion. He was afraid that when they went back to their own dingy looking room they should do so with mixe4 feelings.—Mr. SHAW seconded and the CIIIIIIMIN sup- ported the proposal, which was carried.

div.head: PADGATE SCIIOOLS HO9PITAL.
div.p: PADGATE SCIIOOLS HO9PITAL.

The Superintendent of Padgate Schools (Mr. Mines) reported that the hospital at Padgate Schools, after being unused for two years, was opened on the Friday previous to admit of one patient, but since that date over six had been admitted.—ln answer to a question, the Superin- tendent said the doctor was rather in doubt as to the ailment, but it was supposed to be a mild form of scarlet fever.

div.head: MOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE MOUSE COMMITTEE.

The House Cornneittee recommended that the premises of Mr. John Nortary, situate in Scotland-road, be hired for the No. 1 districb relief office temporarily, where the relieving officer for the No. 1 divrict would attend for the purpose of receiving applications for relief, and also where the Guardians would attend to dispose of relief cases, at the sum of 203. weekly, to cover all charges except cleaning, &c. It was recommended that Miss Mary Lee, aged 18 years, be appointed children's atten- dant, and generally to assist the matron, at the yearly salary of £lB, with the usual lodging rations and wash. Mg, duties to commence on Wednesday, the 21st inst.— The minutes were confirmed.
THE NEWT,I:4 RECHSTRARSHIP.
A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the appointment of Mr. Bowe, relieving, officer, as registrar of births, deaths, and marriages fur the district.
A LOAN.

The Assistant CTk said a letter had been received from Mr. Ashton, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians, asking for the loan of the Board's boxes and bags for use while they were taking their poll with regard to the desirability or otherwise of holding triennial elec- tions in that Union. The Assistant Clerk said he had complied with the request, and his action was approved by the Board.

A NOTICE OF MOTION. Mr. Muir gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that the resolution recently passed limiting the absence of the matron and other officers of Padgate Schools to six hours a week, be rescinded. He was pro- ceeding to give reasons for the motion, but he was ruled out of order by the Chairman. ,

div.head: TENDERS AND CONTRACTS.
div.p: TENDERS AND CONTRACTS.

The Padgate Schools Committee reported that samples of quilts were, submitted to the Committee and it was decided to accept the tender of Mr. Benson for 100 quilts for boys at 33. 61. each, 90 inches by 50 ; and 100 for girls at 4s. 4d. each, 93 inches by 60. The following contracts for the ensuing six months were accepted : Clogs, Mr. Jones; potatoes, Mr. James Warburton ; cord and twill. Mr. Evans; coal and slack, Messrs. Evans and Co.; shoes,Mr. Roberts; glazing, Mr. Pritchard ; brushes, Mr. Chester ; coffins, Mr. Lowden Wells ; stone, War- rington Slate Company; milk (schools), Mr. Floughton ; printing and stationery, Mr. James Wood. Several tenders were referred to various committees of the Board for consideration.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

In the "Clarion" we are told that Warrington made no mistake in their match with the St. Cleincoat's, at Roch- dale, and the writer says" I take it as a good sign that the Wilderspool young men are in sufficiently good form to make a bold bid for the new trophy. By the bye, Warrington used to hold strong opinions concerning cup competitions. They threw the sponge up with disgust after having gone through two seasons for the West Lancashire Cup—a competition that was Principally promoted by Fred T. Parry, of Liverpool. Warrington, at that time, said that cup competitions engendered bad feeling and brutal play, and the ties they competed in certainly bore the stamp of roughness, but I fancy it was mainly through being worsted in the second season's contest that they cried peccavi, as there was nothing unduly rough in the play that I could see."

But the old order changetli and gives way to new.and Warrington, as well as other clubs, will find the govern- ing principle of the present competition a more intelli- gent and a more refined one thin that which rules an old time cup contest. One mistake in the latter settles the hash of a club for the season, but it is impossible to make several mistakes in a competition under the league mode and after all come out champions of th 3 tourney. Then again Warrington have profited by experience since the time of which I write. They have a finer feel- ing of what is needed on a football field, and they have a better sense of how a defeat should be taken, though they are the keenest rivals a club can meet." The same writer is of opinion that the following four clubs will occupy the leading positions in the championship at the end of the season :—Swinton, Warrington, Salford, and Oldham.

At the animal meeting of the Lancashire County Football Club last Wednesday, the scheme for the Lan- cashire County Club Championship was brought for- ward, and passed with a few slight alterations. As most of our readers are aware, the competition will not be really floated until next season. The present competition will, however, go on, and fill the gap, and in the mean- time the necessary arrangements will be made to make the championship competition next year bath complete and comprehensive.

All entries must be in before October 1 this year, and after that the committee will arrange the clubs into classes of ten each, with the exception of the last class, which may be formed of a smaller number. The usual method of promotion in Leagues will 131 observed, the two highest of the second will play the two lowest of the first, and the winners will change places with the losers. •

North End are doing well. Eight points in the first four fixtures is a big improvement on last season, when they were defeated at Nottingham and Burnley in their second and third matches. Notts Forest turned up at Deepdale with a mixed team, but they gave their antagonists a rare good game for all that. They were defeated by a goal to nothing, but they gave such an ex- hibition as delighted the spectators. The Forest style of play is admired everywhere, and there is no doubt they will be an attraction wherever they go.

--- Blackburn Rovers came in for a rare fright in their battle with Everton. You may imagine the shock their supporters had when the second half was slipping away, and the Evertonians were leading by two goals to none. It was left to two of the old hands, Forest and South- worth, to save the club's colours, the end of a fierce game being a draw. Derby Arthur was again in the Rovers' goal, whilst Pinnell took the place of the disabled Jar- dine at the other end.

The League Clubs were again very fortunate on Saturday in the matter of weather. It could hardly have been better, football being seen under the best possible meteorological conditions, and the attendances were again large, as the following list shows : Perry Barr i Villa v. Suntleaind Nottingham: County v. Derby County 12,000 Blackburn 3 Hovers V. Bretton Preston: North Bad v. Notts Forest. B,OOO Burnley : Bnrnley v. Newton Heath 7,060 Bolton : Wanderers V. Sheffield Wednesday Stoke: Stoke v. Accrington West Bromwich : Albion v. Wolverhampton Wands 5,000 Total , 67,000 ' Of the eight games in the First Division of the League, Aston Villa were the only home team to be beaten. And what a beating it was! Prior to Saturday they ha'l only lost one goal in their League engagements,but now, alas! they had no fewer than six chalked up against them. Sunderland were in irresistible form, actually scoring three goals inside the first 15 minutes. With , the champions going in this style, no wonder that the play of the Villa was described as "wretched," " aw- fully weak," Sze., the spectators being wofully disap- pointed after they had flattered themselves that the Villa were the greatest team on earth. AT WARRINGTON.

MR. YATES'S REPLY TO MR. BRIGHOUSE. Mr. IL C. Yates, coroner for the Enutsford divi- sion of Cheshire, held two inquests on Saturday afternoon at the hospital of the Manchester Ship Canal at Latchford, which is situated beyond • the boundaries of the borough of Warrington, and in conversation with a newspaper representative, he expressed surprise at the remarks of Mr. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, with reference to the difficulty which had arisen between them as to holding an inquest at Latchford last week. Mr. Yates explained that it was only very shortly before the incident referred to took place that he was ad- vised by the Clerk of the Cheshire County Council that Latchford had been transferred to Lancashise, and was thenceforth not in his jurisdiction. Mr. Yates naturally coneluded that a similar notification had been sent at the same time by the Lancashire County Council to their coroner, and was therefore surprised to receive the report of the fatal accident in Latchford from Mr. Runt, the chief-constable of Warrington. As a result he wired to the Clerk to the Cheshire County Council, and his former instructions not to hold such inquests were confirmed, which, as already reported, he communicated to the Warrington police. On receiving from Mr. Hunt Mr. Brighouse's letter declining to hold the inquest Mr. Yates wired to the Clerk of the Cheshire County Council a second time, even suggesting that he might hold the inquest in question, hut received instructions not to do so until the Lancashire County Council had been communicated with. A subsequent telegram was received from the clerk by Mr. Yates, stating that the Clerk of the Lancashire County Council thought that Mr. Yates had no jurisdicti3n, and that it was the duty of Mr. Brighouse to hold the inquest, and that the latter had received instructions to do so. With reference to the statement by Mr. Brighouse at the inquest that Mr. Yates appeared to have been holding inquests illegally in Latchford since the passing of the Local Government Act of 1888, Mr. Yates did not think this was the case, as he understood that it was only recently that the Lancashire County Council had received the necessary order from the Local Government Board transferring Latchford to their jurisdiction' without which order Latchford would have continued in Lie district. Mr. Brighouse at the inquest expressed his willingness to hold Latchford inquests if he were legally entitled to do so, and thus it will be seen that the dilemma arose from no fault of his or Mr. Yates, but from the omission of the Lancashire County Council to notify to their coroner as the Cheshire County Council notified to theirs, the transference of Latch lord to Lancashire as soon as the order from the Local Government Board had been obtained. This alteration means to the Latchford jury- men tlae loss of the customary shilling, which the Cheshire county allowed each of them.

div.p: 4EyisioN COURTS.
WAREINGFTON.

The Revising Barrister, Mr. James Thos. Foard, concluded at the Town Hall, ou. Siturday morning, tis reviehin of ;the list of votera for the Warrington district. Mr. John Clayton, Liberal registration agent, represented the Liberals, and Mr. Hampson Conservative registration agbnt, the Conservatives' The business was merely formal, and consisted of the checking over of the results previously obtained. At the close Mr. Hampsort said he would like to thank his Honour for the manner in which he had conducted the revision, and considered the claims and objections and The interests of the voters generally. He also thanked the overseers for preparing such good lists, there being fewer claims and objections this year than he had known before since he came to Wm rington.—Mr. Clay. t..an said he thanked his Honour on behalf of the Liberals for the way in which he had conducted the revision. He thought they had got through their work very nicely and easily, and that credit was due to the overseers for their lists, which had been very free from clerical errors. He thought some credit was also due to the printers for their accuracy.—The Revising Barrister said he was much obliged for the thanks accorded to him. He quite agreed with what had been said about the lists by the agents of both parties, because they had got through without much trouble and with the smallest friction. It showed that the lists had been carefully ptepared, and that the printers had done their part towards that end. He thanked the respective agents for their attendance, and the assistance they had given him. He did not think there had been any unnecessary squabbling, and the work had been done in a thorough manner. He was not quite satisfied with the arrangements, with 'regard to the lodger claims. Some of these might not be bond fide, especially in cases where there seemed to be some family arrangement. Of course he must insist on proving these cases, until there was sows alteration in the registration laws.—Mr. TunstaU,, assistant overseer, said he was very much nblige4 to ths, agents for what they had said, so far as , concerned himself. The overseers had tried to do their ' best, and to sonte extent he good lists prepared owed their merits to the information supplied by the agents'. . SANKEY.

Mr. Jqnied,ThottniaßOard. the revising barrister, held a criiiirstaheCrown and Cushion Inn, on Z-faturday, for the,revision of the lists of voters, in the township of Penkeili for the Ireirton- Parliamentary division. Mr. John Holland, of Earlestown, Liberal registration agent, represented the Liberal interest, and Mr. 0. Swift, solicitor, of St. Helens, appeared for the Crmservativas. Two ownership claims were made by James Edgerley in respect of a freehold house, and Robert Taylor in respect of a freehold cottage. Mr. ',Holland objected on be- half of Mr. John KjLinaker, of Sankev-street, Earles- town.—Mr. • Swift said the objector ',Maker was not himself on the ownefshin list, and according to the Act of PArliament lie must be on the ownership register to he entitled to object. Ile was only on the oocupa- tion list. Mr. Swift nientioned that he • had raised this point at St. Helens.--Mr.,Flolland said his 'Honour had accepted last year the saMo form as Wa4 put in now.— The Revising Barriater said' thlticibleatiOn was not to the Fottii but to the man who objected. The point had hot been taken previously. The difficulty had not arisen before:—Mr. Swift said that was because there had always been a good objection to a claim in itself.—Mr. Holland asked his Honour to reserve his decision, RS if he now decided that Mr. Swift's conten- tion was right a great many claims would be affected. His Honour read the section bearing on the case, and said he was inclined t 4 think Mr. Swift was right, and would allow the claims, subject to his not subsequentlr discovering that later Acts of Parliament annulled what he had read.—There was no other business of interest.

On Saturday evening Mr. Foard held a sitting at the Borough Police Court for the purpose of revising the lists of voters in the townships of Rixton, Glazebrook, Pool- ton-with-Fearnhead, Woolston, and Warrington extra municipal, in the Newton Parliamentary Division. Mr. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, appeared on behalf of the Cong.rvatives, and Mr. Holland, Earlestown, represented the Liberals. The oversoers for the several townships were also present. The business was of a very formal character, and nothing transpired which was of public interest.

div.head: SOUTH LEEDS ELECTION.
div.p: SOUTH LEEDS ELECTION.

Messrs. J. L. Walton (Liberal), R. J. Neville (Conser- vative), and Mahon (Labour) were on Tuesday nomi- nated for the Parliamentary vacancy in South Leeds. After the nominations had been handed in, an objection' was lodged against Mr. Mahon, on the ground that owing to incorrectness of a nominator's name an d address his nomination was invalid. The Mayor allowed the objection. RESULT OF THE POLL.

The election of a member of Parliament for South Leeds, to fill the vacancy caused by the elevation to the peerage of Sir John Lyon Playfair, took place on Thurs- day. The candidates were Mr. J. L. Walton (L) and Mr. R. J. Neville (C). Large crowds gathered round the committee rooms and polling booths, and the excitement was of such a, character as has not been witnessed in Leeds for many I years. There was a great rush of voters to the polling booths (luring the dinner hour, and large crowds assem- bled at the street corners, and eagerly discussod the I aspect of affairs. The representatives of the Labour party took no part in the contest. The poll closed at eight o'clock amidst great excite- ment. Many voters arrived too late to record their votes The ballot boxes were immediately conveyed to the Town Hall, where the counting took place. Several trap accidents °centred during the day, the most serious befalling Councillor Laycock, a . prominent Liberal, who was thrown out of his conveyance and severely shaken. The result was declared last night as follows : Walton (L) Neville (C) • Liberal majority 943 The figures at the general election were— Sir Lyon Playfalr (1.) R. J. Neville (C) 3294

LICENSING AT WARRINGTON.-MAGISTRATES' DISSENT.

Sir,—My public duties as Med;cal Officer of Health prevented me from adding my vote to the minority against the granting of additional licenses to the rich monopoly of Messrs. Greenell, Whitley, and Co. If I had been present I should have given the following reasons for my vote :-Ist. The Licensing Bench, having regard to the wants of the neighbourhood,should have re- fused any or all of the licenses offered as "a bribe." 2ndly. The question of granting fresh licenses was a

matter that ought to have been considered entirely apart from the delusive offer of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley,and Co. 3rdly. had the Licensing Committee been satisfied that the wants of the neighbourhood required new hotels, and had a desire to mete out even-handed justice all round, they would have granted Mr. Bolton's appli- cation in Battersby-lane, and The Grove in Bewsey-road. --Yours, kc.,
JOHN H. GORNALL. Warrington, 22nd September, 1892.

Sir,—l shall be glad if you will allow me, through the medium of your paper, to express my dissent from the decision arrived at by the majority of magistrates on Tuesday. The granting of tho provisional licenses to two new houses to be erected in Bewsey-road, and Battersby-lane, is to my mind an injustice done to the districts, whose inhabitants did not ask for, nor do they want these houses. This may not apply to some of the people ; but the evidence before us clearly indicated that the majority of the householders are opposed to the introduction of these licensed houses. Had the contrary been proved, then, in all fairness, the "Grove" in Bewsey-road, and Mr. Bolton's house in Sattersby-lane, had the first claim on the consideration of the Bench. These houses have only out-door licenses, which are said to be greater sources of evil than full licenses. This being the case, I ask why allow the greater evils to exist and add to them two fully licensed houses ? Why give Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., two new licenses, and refuse to fully license the two already in existence? li we must have public-houses, then the Grove" and Mr. Bolton's house would have met the requirements of the neighbourhoods. But no, in the wisdom of the majority of the magistrates these old houses must con- tinue as they were, and have no favour shown to them, whereas Messrs. Greenall,Whitley, and Co. are permitted to take possession of these districts to the financial damage of those who have fsr so many years been on the ground, and, I fear, to the very serious moral damage of the people. But why this injustice? The only reason, unless we are to go into the comparative quality of liquors sold by Mr. Bolton and his competitors, is that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. offered to give up six old licenses in ituttermarket for the new ones. And the majority of magistrates have persuaded themselves to believe that by accepting this offer they are consulting the best in- terests of the town! The touses remaining in Butter- market-st. are to be enlarged, and will probably do as much or more business, than those given up. But the argument is that larger and finer houses are less damag- ing to the morality of the people than small and tumble- down places. I fear this is not the case, and I can point to several large and well built places which contribute not a little to the drunkenness of the town.

But, for the sake of argument, let us suppose that Buttermarket-st. is to gain. Is this, I ask, any reason for introducing new houses into districts already more than sufficiently provided for, and amongst an unwilling people? By those who have carefully considered the question, it is thought that one licensed house to every 1,000 of the inhabitants Is quite enough to meet all the legitimate requirements of the people. Without having the exact figures before me. I should say Warrington has one license to every 200 to 300. But it will be said we have only given two licenses and taken away six, thus decreasing the number by four. This may look very well on paper, but as I have endea- voured to show does rot fairly describe the transaction into which the magistrates have entered. On the con- trary, I fear the enlarged houses in Buttermarket-st. will be as potent for evil as the larger number of small ones. And two large places are to be created in new districts. This is to me a most extraordinary way of reducing licenses, and of seeking to promote the morality of the town.—Yours truly,
E. J. GUEST.

div.head: TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
div.p: TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS.

Sir,—" To this complexion are we come at last !" We ratepayers of Runcorn, Frodsham, He!shy, and Appleton are so ignorant, it seems, that a special Instruction Class is to be formed with Professor Heywood as prin- cipal, and Professors Brandreth and Williams as assist- ant masters, to educate us a little better on a subject in which we are lamentably ignorant, simply because they are finding out that the ratepayers do not see eye to eye with them, nor swallow all for gospel that they say as to the advantages to be derived by the adoption of Triennial, as against the annual,election of Guardiaas as at present. Mr. Heywood in a speech which he made on the occasion said—" Nothing had occurred to shake his faith in the advisa: ility of the change." Certainly not. Every mother thinks her child the finest in the world, and I do not see why Mr. Heywood should be an excep- tion with his bantling.

--But, sir, I should like to ask Mr. Heywood this ques- tion ; suppose his faith is not confirmed by practice and it is deemed advisable after a trial to recur to the former state, how are we to go back without incurring similar expenses to the present? Mr. Brandreth said that an impression had got abroad that the Guardians had cooked the matter. That the joint has been cooked at Dutton is beyond question, but that all the Guardians have been parties to it I do not believe (indeed I know it is not so) but that the scheme has originated in the futile brains of two or three is equally true. Now, sir, in plain English the only reason they can have in my opinion for the course they have taken is to avoid their coming before the ratepayers every twelve months aud giving an account of their stewardship. ' Sir, in my opinion this scheme has originated in the wrong Place. If the inhabitants of any particular township or townships in public meetings had memori- alized the Guardians for the change, then I could under- stand the Board taking action in the matter. But I cannot understand their present procedure unless to serve some ulterior object. And I do not believe in their professions of economy in advocating the change. It is all bosh. But I shall be much deceived if the public agree to the change, and allow these gentlemen to run away with the bit between their teeth for three years. In former letters I have argued against the adoption of the alteration as quite uncalled for, and I, like Mr. Heywood, have heard nothing which would induce me to change my mind; nay, I am coavinced that if a majority of the ratepayers assent to the alteration it would be one of the ereatest misfortunes that could befall us. But, sir, in spite of what Mr. Heywood says of the ignorance of the ratepayers, I have confidence in their intelligence, so much as to believe that they will be the last parties in the world to do anything to restrict that freedom which they at present possess.—l am, sir, yours truly, SCRUTATOR. Frodsham, Sept. 14th, 1892.

div.head: INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY.
div.p: THE INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY.

Sir,—! have looked, and looked in vain, for more than 50 years of political life, for the independent labour party, and it seems to me I am as far from gratifying my longings now in seeing that party, as I was in 1839, when first I began to struggle for political emancipation. Certainly there have been great advances and improve- ments in the political condition of the working-man in the interval ; but by whom have they been brought about ? Certainly not by the indepehdent labour party— not by the Tory- party—but by the Liberal party, who have done more, and who will do more, for the ameliora- tion of the labouring classes than the Tories. Such being the ease, as past experience proves, it would then be 'wise on the part of the toilers, to give their political

support to that party in the State, who have been their best friends in the past, and from whom they may expect most in future. I want the phrase "Independent Labour Party" explained. I look upon the independence as a myth and mischievous. Was it independent labour that prevented Mr. Forrest from being elected for Salford, and put in a Tory ? Did they remember that Tory's attitude in connection with the strike of the gas stokers in Salford ? If so, and if such is their independence, I shall fight shy of it. It is mischievous—and they are not slow to boast of their power for mischief. Does the independent labourer look upon a seat in Parliament, or en the Town Council, with all election expenses paid, and a good salary att ched, as a thing within his reach, and worth agitating for? Then let him attach himself to the party most likely to help him to this desirable state of things—Arch, Abraham (Mabon) Broadhurst—(he is not in this Parliament, more the, pity, because he had the courage of his opinions, and showed his independence, and suffered for it). Burt, Fenwick, the Wilsons, and others identify themsehr with the Radical party, and have been elected by that party for their statesmanship and political worth. I should say it is not the man who causes the loss of a comparatively safe seat to the party by opposing a good and tried man who, but for him, would succeed and carry the seat ; he may by his stubborness and obstinacy damage the party, and by so doing put back the politi- cal clock, and retard the passing of good measures ; but this is sheer mischief. You may call it independence— call it what you like ;it is mischief, spite, and revenge, because certain crotchets are not answered to his satis- faction and that of his clique, who may be, at most, 10 percent. of the constitroncy. It is not by violently thnusting himself forward that he will win a seat any- where, either in Parliament, Town Council, or on the Lewis bequest. When the people want him they will fetch him out if he is worth having; in the meantime let him " learn to labour and to wait."—l am sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, Sept. 15th, 1892.
CYMRO.

THE SAGE OF t'ENKETH ON EVOLUTION. Sir,—Your correspondent " Theebaw "has hit upon a happy phrase when he designates Mr. Peers the "Sage of Penketh." Such an honorary position entails great responsibilities; and these cannot be maintained by smart sayings and pert insinuations regarding the per- sonality of an opponent. In addition there most be an impartial discussion of the subject on its merits ; and this requires the profoundest efforts of human reason. The Sage of Penketh in his last letter can scarcely be said to rise to the full dignity of the honour so recently bestowed upon him. He says he knows "no source of information so reliable as the logical deductions from the observations of nature." Now, the Sage of Penketh ought to know that deductions are made from theories and general principles, and that, on the other hand, inductions are drawn from the observation of the facts of nature. To a hovice such a distinction may appear a trivial one, but to a logician, well acquainted with his subject, the distinction is crucial and fundamental as it refers to the great difference between the inductive and deductive methlds of science. The Sage of Penketh, however, entirely ignores this distinction, and by doing so unintentionally reveals on his part one of those lacume in his scholarship which prove so fatal and dis- tructive to all his efforts to pose before the public as a scientific authority. It is also curious to find the Sage of Penketh advocat- ing the claims of the anti-vivisectionists OA moral grounds. Now, he himself maintains that natural phen- omena are the result of natural laws; and he must of course as a consequence hold that the laws of nature are necessary and immutable. As an evolutionist, moreover, he must regard man as evolved from the lower creatures. But nature's great , law amongst the animal tribes is the struggle for existence, and the consequent survival of the fittest. But how can he on logical grounds exclude man from the operation of the very same laws? Why amongst humankind should there not be a struggle for existence; and if the cat plays with its victim ere it is devoured, why should not the same laws hold place regarding man? If the Sage regards man as a distinct species, sui generic, then it is easy to see why moral laws should dominate the natural.but if man is linked on by evolution to the lower animals, it becomes very difficult to see how man can act differently to the animals. On such a view, man can only be regarded as a highly specialized animal. It is very fortunate for the Sage of Penketh that the fate of his intellectual offspring does not at times trouble him to any extent. The absenceof the paternal emotion was specially manifested on a late occasion, when in an ill-fated hour he fiercely and furiously baptized one offspring of his brain as a red-herring. Such conduct can scarcely be called compatible with one occupying the honoured position of the Sage of Penketh, even were he to undertake to spice these highly coloured bantlings, (to use his choice phrase on a previous occasion) with the "flavour of dignity, honour, and earnestness."— Yours, Igc., September 19th, 1892.
A LEARNER.

div.head: BURTON WOOD COUPLE AGAIN.
div.p: THE BURTON WOOD COUPLE AGAIN.
THE DEFENDANT CUTS HIS THROAT IN
COURT.

At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednes- day before Mr. John Crosfieid (chairman), and Mr. S. R. Armitage, Jeremiah Chenery, was charged with assaulting his wife, Catherine Chenery, at Burton- wood, on the 13th inst. Mr. Webster, of St. Helens, defended. The complainant stated that she saw her husband coming home, and as she had heard he had a revolver, she locked him out, and he tried to break the door in, and broke the windows, throwing stones through them at her and striking her with a brush. —ln reply to Mr. Webster the complainant admitted that she had been bound over to keep the peace for assaulting her husband last month. She had constantly refused him admission to the house, because he threatened to kill her. She said he had money and she had none, and that made the difference. He was collecting all over for cork legs, and all sorts of things. (Laughter.) She had never maltreated and threatened him. There was another woman at Southport that he kept writing to, and he read to people her letters. Witness was quite sure there was not another man in the case. Her hus- band became quite wild sometimes, and on the day in question kept calling out "take me to Rainhill." She made application for a judicial separation, saying she would not live with him to be killed.—Mr. Webster said this seemed to be a case of an unfortunate Marriage. (The Complainant : Yes, it is.) His client had been most unfortunate, and since he lost his leg his wife seemed to think that now she had only got part of a man to live with, she thought she would do her best to get rid of him. She had been bound over for cutting , open his head with a brick on the 25th ult. On the day in question when she locked him out she exasperated him by behaving in a m•.st unseemly and disgusting Tnanner in the house, he observing her trough the window, and struck him through it with a broom, breaking a pane. He seized the broom and took it from her, and then he foolishly broke several panes of glass. He was on the club of the Miners' Permanent Relief Society, and only received Sc. 7d. a week.—The Bench fined the defendant ss. and costs. and made an order for separation and an allowance of 2s. a week to the wife.—The d :endant excitedly striking the partition of the dock with his stick exclaimed that he would not pay one halfpenny ; he would die first. He was put back to a seat by the police, still exclaiming noisily, and suddenly he pulled a knife from his pocket and drew it across his throat, but before he had inflicted more than a slight cut,a constable took the knife from him.—The defendant exclaimed a number of times in an excited voice : " I wish I could do it," and added, "She has behaved like a brute to me."—The Chairman remarked that a medical man had better be sent for to certify as to the defendant's condition. The best thing for him would be to tend him to an asylum. —Mr. Webster observed that perhaps the injury to the defendant's head by his wife had affected his brain.— Dr. Peacocke subsequently examined the man and pro- nounced that he was not insane, and as he declined to pay the fine, he was conveyed to prison.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

THEFT M A LYMM MAN.—William Brookes, who lives with his mother at Rush Green,Lymm,was apprehended by the Lymm police, on a warrant for having stolen a scythe, hammer, and whetstone, the property of Thomas Cartwright, Tittensor, Staffordshire. He was handed over to the Staffordshire police. THANKSGIVING bERVICES.—On Sunday the annual harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lymm, when the sermons were preached by Mr. Hale, of Manchester College. On Mon- day, a service of song, entitied " Seedtime and Harvest," was rendered by the choir,and an address was also given by Mr. Weffry, of Lymm. There were very fair con- gregations at all the services. THE VOLIIINTEERS.—On Saturday, the Lymm Volun- teers, under the command of Lieutenant Groves, as- sembled at the Cross, ana marched, headed by the band, to Thelwall. They called at the residence of Mr. R. A. Naylor, where they were supplied with refreshments. They then proceeded home again. On Sunday morning they acain assembled at the Cross, and marched to Warburton Church, where Divine service was held. There was a good muster of men at each parade.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1892. DOWN BY THE SEA.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1892. DOWN BY THE SEA.

[WITHOUT THE EASSINETTE.] EY JOHN PEERS. (Continued.) My meeting with the gentle evangelist—the lady of many tracts—a lady—despite the well-worn gloves and general "other worldiness' of her attire —led me to reflect upon the fact that a trip like this might be looked upon as a small microcosm—a little of the world in little. What a variety of faces, coupled with such a variety of manner and disposi- tion! What a contrast, for instance, between the , gentle soul who evinced so much interest in my eternal welfare—and the " Arries" who, loud in voice and costume, are for ever making their offen- sive presence only too evident. " Arry's" ideal of the "whole duty of man" appears to be to cram as , much swagger and vulgar effrontery into his manner I and discourse as possible: the impersonation of selfishness and self-conceit. Whereas she, in her self-abnegation has devoted her life and leisure to accomplish what she thought to be the welfare of others. Although neither could claim to be pro- digies of ratiocination, and though both lives, it appeared to me, were founded upon the insecure base of unreason, my sympathy was as great for the one as was my abhorrence for the other. Yes! I am persuaded the world would be all the sweeter, were there only a few more women in it like my gentle monitress. Nothwithstanding the tracts, and the zealous persistency with which she continued to pour more or less appropriate texts into my left ear—which, I am ashamed to confess, ' took immediate flight out of the right—thereby adding one more illustration of the emptiness of the intervening space—in spite of all this society would be distinctly better for a large admixture of this serious unselfish simplicity. And even for her antithesis—the blatant and ob- trusive " Arry''—some facts for our consideration might be advanced to mitigate the severity of our adverse judgment in his case. Doubtless he is the product of one phase of our boasted civilization; and the tree can not be wholly good that produces such evil fruit. Consider his case. Bound by the exigency of business to spend his time in unthink- ing routine—compelled to work as a more or less intelligent machine, what chance has he for im- provement of mind and manner? His days are one monotonous round of paid slavery; his leisure fri- volous if not debasing recreation. All this points to a want of social moral sanitation. _
And now, to thee, my sweet evangelist, farewell, a long farewell. May the heaven thou so often im- portunes for the benefit of others, be thy meed at last!

In a miscellaneous collection of beterogenous individuals like this of ours, some are certain to exhibit their inherent propensity to go wrong, or— what is, on the rails, nearly as bad—fail to go right. This was the case with two very pleasant young ladies and an elderly gentleman,who, for a consider- able time sat opposite me—tlie girls laughingly en- gaged in writing to some absent friend—they being evidently ardent disciples and strict folkwers of "Captain Cuttle," busying themselves in taking notes by the way. This pleasant diversion—which my experience tells me too often results in the pro- duction of illegible hieroglyphics—was abruptly terminated by the information that they had over- shot their changing place by some station or two.

_ Now, why are not we, as well as our luggage, labelled? Why shou'd our impedimenta—our trunks, valise, oe bandbox--go safely and surely on to its appointed destination, while we, unhappy that we are, sit kicking our heels at some out-of-the-way roadside station, mourning the loss of the departed and disturbing the placid meditations of local offi cialdom by our supplications to be re-united there- to. Speaking for myself, feelingly, I think there is f.,..eater need for labelling ourselves than there is for docketing a box or a parcel. This will never go astray of its own volition; it is all right until some wrong-headed person mis-directs it or mis- takes it for his oven,and so mis-appropriates it; but we often do get astray by following our own lead- ing. If this unhealthy season,and other circumstances which make against a green old age permit, I may see this idea carried out and some other fellow reap- ing the benefit,and the blessings of hitherto belated and bewildered passengers. By the adoption of this brilliant idea—l say brilliant for there is gold in it if properly carried out—by this means you might go to sleep comfortably without having the annoyance of some blatant barbarian in po •ter's clothes bawling "Change for Chowbent,Checkerbe and Bradshawlech," or the fear of finding yourself on the road to Peru when your destination was China. If we are properly labelled, the porter of the future will quietly examine our respective dockets, and, if need be, gently remove us to our appointed places, or if we are right, as per label, leave us to the peaceful enjoyment of nature's sweet restorer.

Cardiff, the port of many nationalities, was not fixed upon as a place pre-eminently adapted for a seaside resort, but as a centre from which certain good geologic " diggings" could be reached. First seeking ou,; my good friend, Mr. Storrie, of the Cardiff Museum, and arranging with him to visit I the famous Penarth beds, where occur the Rheetic fossils, so conspicuous by their absence in our own Museum, I made tracks for bed. Now, it is one thing to go to bed; another to slc cp. The heat was great, although the upper sash , of the window was quite down. This arrangement admitted noise as well as air. And the noise was indeed grievou, . The discordant clang of a most inharinoniou,h lied in irregular bangs for the , benefit of some poor passing soul,rent the distracted air and tortured my no less distracted sense of harmony. This went on bra considerable tir %but, just ere the point of utter distraction was reached, this unmusical din gave place to the performance of most pleasing chimes which filled the air with soothing melody. St. Mary's has at least one of the indispensables to a good church—a good peal of bells well hung. As to the others—as, a good clock, a good sun-dial, and a good weather-cock, true to the meridian— well, all these would be great acquisiti-ms, but seldom found combined in one church. Whatever is to be connected with a church should be minis- ters of, or witnesses to, the truth. Some people to this list might be disposed to add a good parson; but opinions differ so very materially as to what constitutes a good parson that I will not offer mine. For parsons change but these go on for ever. At least this is the case with some church clocks, but there is one, not a thousand miles from the present writer, that when it does go, shows a very indepen- dent spirit and a determination to have a time of its own. Not only is it often before or behind other clocks, but each dial has been known to set up a claim to show the one and only true time, being a small matter of some twe or three hours before or behind its fellows. But this is not in Cardiff. Let us return there. Early the next morning I and my guide, philoso- pher, and friend, found ourselves at Lavernock Station on the way to the aforesaid Rheetic beds. These lie exposed to the wasting wash of the Severn,and so are constantly showing fresh features and fossils. The view from here over the river—or rather the Bristol Channel—was very fine : the opposite shore of Somerset, Devon, and perhaps Cornwall, were faintly outlined. Nearer hand Steepholm and Flatholm, out-lying islands of moun- tain limestone, broke the watery expanse. Lavernock head is a cliff of some one hundred feet high, very steep, perpendicular in fact, and , consists of alternating bands or beds of hard grey ' and hluish limestone, loose marls of various colours, and the black bands of thin shale. These are capped by bands of the lower or white has lime. As might be expeeted, the .loose nature of the interbedding marls, causes very frequent falls of the harder lime- stone on to the beach. Great masses of this and their accompanying marls, to the weight of tons, are pretty constantly falling on to the beach with , great noise. From this the source of the boulders and pebbles on the beach, which in some parts is thickly covered with them, is easily traced. The marls have gone to make the Severn the muddy river I found it to be. Nothing but the hardest rock could withstand the constant rush and pound- ing things get upon this beach. Here the " strike " of the rock beds, i 3 almost directly at right angles with the beach, and the ridges dip into the water, and extend for some considerable distance out— forming the " Race" of Lavernock, broken water somewhat dangerous to navigation. But it is with the beach itself we are more con- cerned. Here we are enabled to walk over the very beds of which this precipitous cliff is composed. Layer on layer the thick-ril.bed limestone bands lie s'ated one over the edge of the other, the exposed ' edges forming steep steps of some three or four feet deep. The limestone band is seldom more than a 1 foot thick, the rest being composed of the softer intervening beds. Between two of these bands,and associated with a black gypsum band, lies a thin bed of black mud, thick coated, and interspersed with fish remains—bones, scales, and teeth. On the surface and embedded in the limestone the Rhcetic

Venus comb frequently occurred. This shell, rejoic- ing in the euphonious name of Pccten Valoniensis, is one et the medals by which this particular series of beds is distinguished from the series above and below it, and is thus one of its characteristic fossils. Hence it was one of the objects of this arduous and adventurous expedition. And upon the smooth and sea-worn faces of these beds the traces of the sun's action can be read even now. Over the whole surface of soma of these the sue-oracks make fantastic patterns. The resulting figure varies somewhat, but, if I remember rightly most nearly approaches the hexagon. These old sun- baked mud beds tell us something of the conditions obtaining at this time when the earth, the offspring of the sun, had attained to middle age.when strange- looking creatures walked these shores and left their bones as evidence of the fact, or clove those ancient waters in search or pursuit of prey. Well, the sun- cracks tell that during these long intervening mil- lions of years the sun has acted much as at present. The fact that the mud did dry, and contracted as it dried, shows us that the atmosphere of that time ' was not saturated with moisture, pointing out or suggesting that considerable tracts of land existed at the time, and that very much the same condi- tions as to contractability in drying existed then as now. All this would seem to teach us the per- sistence of natural law; then as now like causes produce like effocts. The sun shone, the rains fell, and the winds blew probably much as they do now. And even the little grains of sand or mud which formed the bottom of those old waters, were impel- led to act much as they do now—in accerdance with their specific gravity.as is shown in the ripple- like markings here before us. Then, as now the under current tended to raise the bottom—loosely composed of sandy or muddy particles—into wave- like ridges, consisting of a long slope and a steep face, the latter always pointing down stream. By this means the direction of the last current over the particular bed in its soft state may be ascertained. But we might go on to tediousness in showing the similarity of nature's doings then as at present. The lover of oysters naturally imagines that these delicious molluscs were made with a view to his especial delectation. So man,lifted up in his pride, arrogates himself. Here are oysters—or the remains of them—that lived and flourished long ages before there was a man in the world to test and to appre- ciate them. Doubtless they were eaten, but the lord of creation had no part therein. (To be continued.)

div.head: CEIARGb' OF STEALING POTATOES.
div.p: CEIARGb' OF STEALING POTATOES.
ALTERCATION ON THE BENCH.

At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, yesterday, before Aldermen Harrison (chairman), and Wright and Dr. Gornall, Edward Davenport, 88 Bostock-street ; Arthur Hassan, 104, Cartwright- street, Robert Bloomfield, Infectious Diseases Hospital ; William Hart, 16, Bostock-street ; Elizabeth Yates, Bostock-street ; and Thomas Shipley, 44, Aiken-street; all youths, were charged with stealing, between 7 and 8 a.m., on the 13th inst., a quar.tity of potatoes, the property of James Green, farmer, 70, St. James's-street. —Mr. Browte appeared for the prosecution.—Mr. Browne said the field in which the potatoes grew, was near the Infectious Diseases Hospital. The , Sanitary Committee had taken the field 1 which was at the back of the hospital, for the pur I pose of putting up an iron hospital, and arrang- meats were made between the Corporation and the owner, Mr. Green, that all the potatoes on the land, whether his own or that sold to the Corporation, should belong to him. All the people in the neighbourhood seemed to think they could go helter skelter among these potatoes and bring them away. 70 yards of potatoes had been cleared away by them. The prisoners had been carrying them away in sacks.—James Green, his brother Richard Green, farmer, Lovely-lane, and P.C. Tur- ner gave evidence confirming Mr. Browne's statement. The latter said he saw the defendants putting the potatoes into sacks, and caught flassall, from whom he got the names of the others. The constable said the defendants admitted being on the field, but said others told them they could take the potatoes, several of them stating that Mr. Bloomfield, keeper at the Infectious Diseases Hospital, told them they could have them.—Dr.Gornall subjected the witnesses to much cross-examination with a view to elicit that the potatoes had been taken from near the hospital,of which the Cor- poration had possession. He remarked that the defen- dants ought to be defended by some one, and he felt more like an advocate for them, as being constantly on the spot he knew what had been going on.—Wm.B.srton deposed that the defendantßloomf 31d,son of the keeper at the hospital, worked with him from 6 30 till dinner time on the 13th inst.—Mrs. Yates, mother of the defendant Yates, said her son came in and told her they were giving potatoes in the Corporation field, and Mr. Bloom- field had given permission. She went to him and asked him if he had, and he said he had not, but they could have all the potatoes on the ground, though they were no good.—Dr. Gornall was making some remarks at this point. when Mr. Browne observed that he did not know whether that gentleman was the witness or the witness herself.—Dr. Gornall: It joins close to where lam two or three times a day and I can't be there so much with- out knowing something about the matter.—Mr. Bailey gave evidence in favour of Hassall, an'u said there had been hundreds of people carrying potatoes in sacks from the ground, and it was unfenced and was a regular play-field for all the children round about. Almost all the lads said the potatoes had been given them to take them off the ground. In reply to Dr. Gornall he said he saw two men with a fork clearing them out on Satur- day.—Dr. Gornall said there were none there on Satur- day except those Mr. Green was not entitled to, because the Corporation had taken possession of the land. He added that he did not think that if he had not happened to be there that morning Bloomfield would have got justice. Ile thought that lad ought to be dismissed at once from the box. He had been proved innocent.— Alderman Harrison : I don't think it makes any differ- ence whe.,her he remains five minutes or not. He is not quite blameless.—Dr. Gornall : He is entirely blameless —Alderman Harrison said there was a technical offence, and there ought to be some nominal penalty inflicted.—Dr. Gornall : I think it is a disgrace to keep Bloomfield in tho box a moment longer. He is proved not to have been present. I can bring witnesses myself to prove that he was in the house at night. His brother has proved he was at work that morn- ing.—Alderman Wright: We quite agree with you that he is innocent.—Dr. Gornall: Then why doesn't the Chairman dismiss him 7—Alderman Harrison said he was there to conduct the business in a proper manner, and he should not allow Dr. Gornall to dictate to him as to what he should do.—Dr. Gornall: He ought to be dismissed.— Alderman Harrison said it was a pity Dr. Gornall did not go into the box. It was more an advocate's part than that of a member of the Bench to act as a partisan in that court. As for his observation that if he had not been there, there would not have been justice done, he indignantly repudiated that. Dr. Gor- nail : You have not dune your duty in not dis- missing him—Alderman Harrison: We should have acted justly whatever had been the consequence, and been guided entirely by the evidence.—Dr. Gornall : I am very glad I have come. I have not wasted my time, though I have other duties to perform.—Mr. Browne applied that the summons be amended to a charge of damage, remarking that there was evidently a mistake on the part of the defendants ; and this desire was acquiesced in.—Dr. Gornall asked the prosecutor whether he had really lost sixpence through the de- fendants ; and he replied that he had.—Dr. Gornall : Don't you think it will requite you what you get from the Corporation ? Alderman Wright: We cannot enter into that. We have had evidence of £5 damage.—Bloomfield was dismissed, and the other defendants were discharged on payment of costs; and Dr. Gornall then left the bench.—Mr. Richard Green stated that the field was fenced with barb wire ; and the Chairman told him him he ought to have said that in evidence.—The Chief Constable said £3O worth of dam- age had been done by people to the field, and Mr. It. Green said it was scandalous his brother bad to stand out of this. Mr. William Bloomfield, of Aikin-street, writes as to this case denying that he gave permission to anyone to take potatoes out of the field. SIR ALBERT ROLLIT ON THE RECENT

div.head: FINANCIAL FAILURES.
div.p: FINANCIAL FAILURES.

-- At a meeting of the Chambers of Commerce on Tues- day, at Newport, Mon., Sir Albert Rollit, M.P., in his presidential address, spoke of the prevailing depression is trade, which was caused by wild speculation followed by contraction of credit. Alluding to the failures of banks and building societies, he said the recent events suggested that every precaution ought to be taken aaainst the plunder of the poor and the consequent injury to national providence and thrift.

div.head: MURDEFI: IN WALES.
div.p: THE MURDEFI: IN WALES.

-- Little doubt now exists that Mary Connolly, the young woman who was found dead at Abergevenny on Friday night, was the victim of foul play. and the police are believed to have her murderer in custody. On Sun- day a labourer named Thomas Edwards, about 30 years of age, surrendered at Abergavenny Police Station, and said he cut Connolly's throat with a razor. The police, acting upon the information which he gave, found the razor hidden by the roadside._

div.head: FREE EDUCATION IN RUNCORN.
div.p: FREE EDUCATION IN RUNCORN.
HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS.

In accordance with the Education Act the state- ment of the income and expenditure of this school is affixed at the main entrance, and the following figures Pre taken therefrom :-Income: Annual grant from Education Department, £405 2s. 6d.; voluntary contributions from private individuals, £lB 18s. 4d. ; collections in church or chapel, £4 Bs. Od.; school pence, £lOB 2s. id. ; paid by Guardians for twelve scholars, £3 13s. 11d. ; amount received from books and other articles sold, £2 18s. 5d.; Fee Grant Fund (section 6), £l7B 10s. Od.; from other sources, hire of room, cheques, bazaar, &c., £lB2 13s. Od.; total, £904 6s. 3d. Expenditure: By balance 30:h June, 1892, £7O 9s. 5d.; salaries of teachers, boys, £169 4s. Od., girls, £125 16s. Od., infants, £B7 7s. 9d., total, £382 7s. 9d.; salaries of assistants. boys, £l2B Os. Od., girls, £55 2s. 2d. ; infants, £56 9s. 5d., total, £239 11s. 7d.; salaries of articled pupil teachers, £3B 11s. 6d.; temporary moni- tors, £5 is. Od.; hooks, apparatus, and stationery, £52 3s. 4d.; fuel, light, and cleaning, £42 2s. 5d.; replacement of furniture, repairs to building, &c., £46 19s. 6d.; rent, 2s. ; rates, taxes, and insurance, £9 Os. 6d. ; bank commission and interest, £5 12s. id. ; postage, carriage, printing, and advertising, £l2 ss. 2d. ; total, £904 6s. 3d. The report of H.M. Inspector of ' Schools is open for inspection from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. at the School, but as it was considerably after the latter hour when our representative called, he had not the op- portunity of seeing the document. At the same time it may be stated that Mr. T. FL Annett, the head master, argued that " inspection " did not include copying for publication, and that he should refuse to allow the report to be copied, but any ratepayer was quite at liberty to inspect it. This objection has not been raised at the other schools, and their reports have been pub- lished in this journal.
HOW DENOMINATIONAL EDUCATION IS MAINTAINED. BY A RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

For the first time the ratepayers of Runcorn have this year been enabled to ascertain the finan- cial position of the denominational schools of Run- corn : and the statements of accounts as published in the " Examiner " have been highly interesting reading. On the occasions of School Board elections we have been accustomed to hear those connected with these schools speak of the self-sacrifices they have had to make to maintain them. The gross iniquity of taxing these gentlemen with a School Board rate, when in addition they had to subscribe to keep their own schools, has been depicted in language calculated to rouse the feelings of fair play existing in every Englishman's breast, and thus enlist his sympathy. But of course these gentlemen were willing to submit to these sacrifices in order that the rising generation might continue to be taught the religious faith of their forefathers, and also that the rates might be kept as low as possible. In the light of the statements of accounts for the year ended 30th June last, this has evidently been so much " blarney "—so much dust thrown in the eyes of the ratepayers, and that it has served its purpose is seen by the fact that there sit on the School Boards of Runcorn and Widnes a majority of gentlemen pledged to support denominational schools and who are thus managing schools belong- ing to the ratepayers, with the work of which schools they have no sympathy. Taking the three principal denominational schools in Ruacorn, I find that the self-sacrificing gentle- men of the Parish Church Schools subscribed the sum of £5B 14s. during the past year, and that the ' collectlon plate in church added the further amount of £lB, making a total of voluntary contributions of £76 14s. The total income of these schools was no less than £1,384 ss. 7d., and as the voluntary sub- eriptions were so meagre, compared with this large amount, whence catne the rest? Government supplied the munificent sum of £1,021 12s. 6d. in grants, and the parents of the children attending the schools were taxed to the tune of £236 18s., notwithstanding the "Free Education" Act of a Tory Government. In the Brunswick Wesleyan School the proportion be- tween the public money and the private contributions is even greater. Here the supporters of denominational education subscribe £ll 10s. of a total income of £930 Bs. 4d. As in the previous case, the Government sup- plies the bulk, the grants amounting to £685 10s, and the parents were taxed in school pence to the sum of £l5O Us. 2d., although there was a balance in hand at the commencement of the year of £l9 13s. 6d., which at the end of the twelve months had increased to £4O 2s. 3d. This balance might usefully and justly be dissi- pated in reducing the fees of the scholars for the present year. _

At Holy Trinity School the subcribers contributes 218 18s. 4d. to an income of £904 6s. 3d. The collec- tion in Church realised £4 Bs., and the sum of £lB2 13s. 10d., is put down to "hire of room, cheques, bazaar, &c.," which appears to have been used in meeting the ordinary expenses of the school. The grants from the Government amount to £583 12s. 6d., and scholars had to pay in pence the sum of £lOB 2s. Id. So that even in this case, taking into account the bazaar money, there is a wonderful difference bAween the income from private sources and from the public funds. , The lesson to be learned from these figures is quite cl3ar. The schools are almost wholly maintained from the taxes of the country, and their management ought to be in the hands of representatives of the ratepayers, and not under the control of a few individuals in their private capacities. "Taxation without representation is unjust." Perhaps the popular control of schools sus- tained by public money may come in the near future, but until that day arrives it would be well if the rate- payers would send to the School Board men whose only interest is to serve them by making the Board Schools as efficient as possible, and by extending the accommoda- tion as circumstances require,and not men whose central idea is to conserve the interests of the Denominational Schools, and retard the extension of the Board Schools. Man cannot serve two masters, and a Denomina- tional School manager cannot serve the ratepayers to advantage because of his prejudices. Tne voters of Widnes will have to form a new School Board in the middle of October, and those of Runcorn at the beginning of December next, and if they are wise they will return men whose ideas on education are not warped by ' denominational prejudices, but who are desirous and willing to give a good sound education, at the least possible cost. Had it not been for the Denominational- ' ists on the School Board Widnes parents there would, ere this, have been relieved altogether of the payment of ' school fees ; and free education in Runcorn Board Schools was not won without a severe struggle. Those who run may read. These gentlemen would continue to put a tax upon education if they could, and would do it in the name of the Christian religion; but ignorance has been so far driven away, that people are no longer to be frightened by the bogies that in the past have been used with such success, and the cry of a " godless educa- tion " will not have the weight in the coming contest that it once had. The sacred Scriptures are read and prayers offered in the Board Schools of Runcorn and Widnes, but no doctrinal explanation is allowed to be given, and considering how doctrine makes we Chris- tians love one another, doctrine might fittingly be left out of the curriculum of a Denominational School.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH IN A TRAIN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH IN A TRAIN.

Last night, the train rEaching the Central Station, Warrington, at 8-10, brought with it the remains of a woman, between 40 and 50 years of age, who had started from Southport for Urmston in company with her grandson, and had been found dead in the carriage, between Altcar and Lydiate. The corpse had been decently covered, and, with the child, was conveyed to Urmston. We learn that the woman has a husband living, but could not ascer- tain her name.

div.head: ACCIDENT LAST NIGHT.
div.p: ACCIDENT LAST NIGHT.

Mr. Samuel Houghton, farmer, Grappenh all, was standing on a stack at his farm, last evening, and he slipped off, and fell upon the prongs of a hay- fork, which stood against the stack. The fork passed through his shoulder, and a medical man was called in, who pronounced him very seriously injured.
A LADY THROWN AND DROWNED.
Mrs. Gilbert, daughter of Mr. Mitchell Henry, while driving from Kylemore Castle to Derrinver, near Clifden, on Wednesday,was thrown from a phaeton into the river and drowned.

div.head: _ SAD POISONING CASE.
div.p: _ SAD POISONING CASE.
--- Mrs. Howard, a baker's wife, and her daughter died on Wednesday, at Great Ysrtnouth, through eating poisonous fungi in mistake for mushrooms. Mr. Howard is also in a critical condition.
Through the breaking of a rope Henry Bowker, steeple-jack, while pointing a stack near Stockport, on Monday, fell forty yards, and was instantly killed.

A RECTOR FOUND DEAD.
The Rev. T. Holmes, rector of Garthorpe, Melton Mowbray, was yesterday found drowned in a well ad- joining his residence.
BOILER. EXPLOSION.
TWO MEN KILLED.
PARIS, FRIDAY.—A serious boiler explosion occurred in the engine house of a steam saw mill at Chateaulin yesterday. Two workmen were killed, and five others seriously injured.

div.head: FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENTS IN WALES.
div.p: FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENTS IN WALES.

Yesterday a shocking accident was reported from Bryn Amam, Rhondda Valley, where a miner named David Williams fell between a train af seven trucks in the mine and was fearfully mutilated, death being instan- taneous. A hauler named David Jones and a horse were also killed at Llwynypea by a heavy fall of roof.

div.head: WALWORTH MURDER.
div.p: THE WALWORTH MURDER.

At the Old Bailey, yesterday, John James Banbury (22) was sentenced to death for the murder of his sweet- heart, Emma Oakley, at Walworth, by shooting her with a revolver. The crime was the outcome of jealously. It will be rememnered that on Wednesday a jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against the prisoner, with a recommendation to mercy, but that on the fore- man of the jury stating that two of the jurors were deaf and had not heard the evidence, the judge ordered a new trial.
DEATH OF THE DUKE OF SUTHER- LAND.

The Duke of Sutherland died at 10.30 on Thursday night at Dunrobin Castle, from the effects of a chill. The Earl of Cromarty arrived at the castle ten minutes later, and therefore was not in time to see his father pass away. The late Duke was in his 65th year, and had only been ill a few days, no danger being apprehended before Wednesday. He did much to extend railway communications throughout Scotland, having spent over £500,000 in making railways and reclaiming land. He was very popular in the north of Scotland, and his death removes one of th• most public-spirited men of that country. The Marquis of Stafford succeeds to the title. j Iws,

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.
-- 400 DEATHS DAILY AT TEHERAN.

The French Consul at Teheran reports that the deaths there have in a population of 100,000 ranged from three hundred to four hundred a day, and at 'lauds to five hundred a day. The sickness was in all cases appal- lingly sudden, never letting those who were to die from it live into the second day. The members of the Govern- ment and the Governor of the city ran away, and a whole regiment deserted to the country. The dirt and stench from hidden and ill-buried corpses were frightful. The Consul had to bake his own bread, all the bakers having fled. Pilgrimages were resorted to as a means of getting rid of the scourge. The pilgrims died in dozens on the road to the shrines. The French Consul at Tauris has lost his sister and daughter, and his son's tutor has also died.

div.head: MORE DEATHS AT HAVRE.
div.p: MORE DEATHS AT HAVRE.

HAVES, WED NESDAY . —Four persons died of cholera here yesterday, while four fresh cases were reported. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—There were 29 cases of cholera and 16 deaths in Paris and its suburbs yesterday, as compared with 42 cases and 17 deaths on the previous day. Sr. PETERSBURGII, WEDNESDAY.—There were 48 fresh cases of cholera and 16 deaths in this city yesterday, while two patients recovered. ANTWERP, WEDNESDAY.— Mere were four cases of cholera and two deaths here to-thy, BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY. —There were three cases of cholera at Mons to-day, and one death at WASMPS. CRACOW, WEDNESDAY.—Up to the present 32 cases of cholera and 11 deaths have been reported from different parts of Galicia, and the epidemic appears to be slowly spreading. With a view to preventing the spread of the disease, medical regulations are being enforced on the frontier. HAMBURG,WEDNESDAY.—Sixty-four fatal cholera cases occurred yesterday, against 67 on the previous drip.

div.head: FATAL CASE AT HULL.
div.p: FATAL CASE AT HULL.

After a fortnight's immunity from death 'ay cholera in England the Local Government Board reported on Wed- nesday that it had received information from Dr. Mason, the medical officer of health at Hull, that the fireman of the Uranus,who was attacked on Monday, died on Tues- day night of cholera. All precautions are being taken. and the remainder of the crew of the ship are reported well.

div.head: THREATENED STRIKE OF WATEHMEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THREATENED STRIKE OF WATEHMEN AT RUNCORN.

A somewhat serious dispute was threatened between the watermen of Runcorn and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and the matter has received the attention of the Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porters' Association. The complaint is that the company have issued an order intimating their intention to tie up 15 flats, and five crews in the Runcorn section have received a week's notice to terminate their engage- ment. This, it is alleged, is contrary to an agreement of long standing, it having been the rule, when trade was depressed, to find old hands employment on the vessels, whilst younger men were engaged in some other department. Some of the watermen in question have been connected with the Bridgewater Canal Undertak- ing for 30 years, and they have faithfully fulfilled their duties. A meeting of the Watermen's Association was held on Saturday evening, at Runcorn, when the question was considered, after which a deputation was appointed to wait upon Mr. Meadowcroft, the local agent. The large number of members present decided that unless the notices were withdrawn, they would send in their notices to cease work in seven days. This, it is said, will affect about 830 men engaged on the Manchester Ship Canal and the lower and upper reaches of the Mersey. The deputation, on going to the offices of the Canal Company on Monday morning, found Mr. Meadow- croft was away, but it was stated that a telegram should be sent to him, and that his reply should be sub- mitted to them on the followipg day. On Thursday morning, a deputation from the Runcorn branch of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters' Association waited upon the Manchester Ship Canal Company at Runcorn, witl, reference to the dispute which has occurred c—,sequent upon notices being issued for a numbe" of watermen in the company's employ to cease vrk. The dispute was on Thursday morning sett]. d uport.terms which are satisfactory to the men. They have not been made public, but we understand that the company have withdrawn the notices.

PUBLIC NOTICE. THS SHOP ASSISTANTS' HOLIDAY has been granted since March 24th by a large majority of tradesmen. but it is remarkable that it is still refused by afew who could well afford to close on Thursdays at one o'clock. It is also being further endangered by the action of one or two leading tradesmen who are contemplating breaking through the arrangement. We hereby strongly appeal tothe pubic of Warrington and district to decline to purchase after one o'clock.
